title: Meet the bacteria-eating viruses helping fight antibiotic resistance in poultry

content.content: APHA molecular microbiologist Conor Graham reveals how research into bacteria-eating viruses is uncovering promising ways to tackle antibiotic resistance in poultry.
My name is Conor, and I am a microbiologist at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), where I work on developing alternative ways to control bacteria on farms.

One area of my work that I find particularly exciting, is bacteriophage research. The idea that we can use viruses to selectively target harmful bacteria, while potentially leaving beneficial bacteria unaffected, offers an interesting alternative to conventional antimicrobial treatments. My current work is exploring exactly how effective these treatments could be, and how we can investigate them without relying entirely on experiments in live animals.
Why One Health matters

The health of people, animals and the environment is closely connected, a principle known as One Health. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a clear example of why this matters. Every time we use antibiotics, we create opportunities for bacteria to develop resistance. These bacteria can spread between animals, people and the environment, making infections potentially more difficult to treat.

Reducing reliance on antibiotics in livestock is therefore important not just for animal health, but for protecting the effectiveness of these medicines for everyone. Finding alternative ways to control bacterial infections is an important part of this effort.
Using viruses to fight bacteria

Bacteriophages, or phages for short, are viruses that specifically infect bacteria. They attach to the surface of a bacterial cell, inject their genetic material and use the bacterium to produce more phages. Eventually, the bacterial cell bursts, releasing new phages that can infect other bacteria.

Unlike many antibiotics, which can affect a broad range of bacteria, individual phages generally have a much narrower host range. This selectivity is particularly interesting because it means we could potentially target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that make up the gut microbiome.
With antimicrobial resistance becoming an increasing global concern, there is renewed interest in understanding how we might use these viruses in modern veterinary medicine.
Targeting Salmonella Infantis in poultry

My main research focus has been a project investigating bacteriophage treatment against multidrug-resistant Salmonella Infantis in poultry. This work forms part of an international collaboration through the Joint Programming Initiative on Antimicrobial Resistance (JPIAMR), bringing together researchers with expertise in bacteriophages, microbiology and animal health.

Salmonella Infantisis a bacterial pathogen associated with poultry production that can cause illness in people. Some strains carry a large section of additional DNA, called a plasmid, which can be transferred between bacteria. Plasmids can contain genes that make bacteria resistant to multiple antibiotics, including some important antibiotics used to treat infections in hospitals.
Our aim was to investigate whether bacteriophages could effectively control this pathogen, particularly strains carrying these antimicrobial resistance genes.

Initially, potentially useful phages were identified using plaque assays. These are relatively simple laboratory tests that allow us to see whether a phage can infect and kill a particular bacterial strain. However, bacteria do not exist in isolation in the gut. They are part of a complex community of microorganisms, and the surrounding environment can influence how effectively a treatment works.

This is where our work at APHA became particularly important. Our role was to take promising phages identified by the wider research consortium, and investigate their effectiveness in a much more complex system that is more representative of real life.
Recreating the chicken gut without infecting live animals

To do this, we used an in vitro chicken gut model. Rather than experimentally infecting live chickens, this system uses material collected from the caecum, a part of the chicken intestine that contains a diverse community of microorganisms.

The model recreates important features of the chicken gut environment, including its temperature, acidity and lack of oxygen. We introduce bacteria and phages into small vessels containing the chicken gut material, allowing us to monitor how their populations change over time.

The system also uses continuous culture, meaning that fresh nutrients are supplied while waste products are removed. This helps maintain a more stable environment and allows us to study interactions between bacteria, phages and the wider microbiome over several days.

One of the biggest advantages of this approach is that we can investigate potential treatments in a complex biological environment without needing to carry out experimental infections in live animals. We can also collect samples at different time points to investigate not just whether a treatment works, but how it affects the wider bacterial community.
What did we find?

The results were encouraging. Following a single phage cocktail treatment, we observed an approximately 99.9% reduction in Salmonella Infantis. Importantly, this reduction was maintained throughout the remaining three days of the experiment.
We also used DNA sequencing to investigate what was happening to the wider gut microbiome. This allowed us to examine hundreds of different bacterial groups rather than focusing solely on Salmonella.

We found no significant changes in overall microbial diversity following treatment. Although some individual bacterial groups increased or decreased, the broader microbial community remained relatively stable.
This is particularly interesting when compared with conventional broad-spectrum antibiotics, which can affect many different bacterial groups, including those that are beneficial to gut health.

Our findings demonstrate the potential of targeted phage treatment to control an important antibiotic-resistant pathogen while limiting disruption to the wider gut microbiome. They also demonstrate the usefulness of the gut model as a tool for evaluating potential treatments before progressing to animal studies.
Where next?

This research is part of a much wider effort to develop alternatives to conventional antimicrobial treatments. At APHA, we are continuing to explore ways of improving our experimental gut models and incorporating complementary approaches, including intestinal tissue culture, to better understand how treatments interact with the host and its microbiome.

I am also involved in collaborative research through the European Partnership on Animal Health and Welfare, which brings together research institutions across Europe to investigate ways of improving animal health while reducing antimicrobial use. This includes further work investigating bacteriophages against bacterial pathogens such as enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli, a type of E. coli that produces toxins in the gut and can cause diarrhoea.

Phages are not a universal replacement for antibiotics. Bacteria can develop resistance to them, and their narrow host range means that treatments need to be carefully matched to the bacteria being targeted. However, I believe they could become a valuable addition to our approach to controlling bacterial infections.

Ultimately, the aim is not simply to replace one treatment with another, but to develop better ways of preventing and controlling disease. Combining targeted treatments with surveillance, vaccination and improved farm management could help reduce antimicrobial use, improve animal welfare and tackle antimicrobial resistance as part of a wider One Health strategy.

title: What the new UK-EU SPS agreement means for food and feed safety and food businesses

content.content: Cymraeg
Today, it was announced that the UK and EU have agreed a new deal for trading food, agricultural goods, animals and plants between the UK and EU, at a joint Summit in Brussels.

It’s called the UK-EU Sanitary and Phytosanitary Agreement, or SPS Agreement, and was negotiated by the UK Government, led by the Cabinet Office and Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra). You can read the government's full announcement on GOV.UK.

As the SPS agreement is implemented, the FSA’s priority remains the same as it has always been: protecting public health and protecting consumers, by upholding the high food and feed safety standards in the UK.

The agreement will make trade with the EU simpler and smoother, and open up new opportunities to access EU markets for businesses in the future. It will also make it quicker to get fresh produce on the shelves for shoppers.
All sectors in scope of the agreement will need to ensure their products meet EU rules, so food and feed businesses may need to make some changes, even if they don’t currently trade with the EU.
I want to take this opportunity to explain what this agreement means and what businesses should do now.
What is changing?

Right now, food, agricultural goods, animals and plants are subject to controls such as checks or inspections when they cross the border between Great Britain (GB) and the EU. The new agreement will remove most of these controls, making it easier and cheaper for businesses to trade between GB and the EU. Changes to the Windsor Framework will also make it easier for goods to move between GB and Northern Ireland.

The application date for the SPS agreement will be 1 March 2028. From this date, most food and animal feed in GB will need to comply with EU rules. Businesses operating in these sectors may need to make changes, even if they don’t currently trade with the EU.

Food and feed already on the GB market (including stock in storage awaiting sale) before 1 March 2028 can still be sold and used in GB until stocks run out, even if they don’t meet EU rules. This stock must not enter the EU – we will provide further guidance to help businesses and local authorities keep this stock in the GB market.

Will food be as safe as before?

The FSA's role is, and continues to be, to protect public health and protect the interests of consumers. We will continue to make decisions based on evidence, and support safe, new and innovative technologies so that the high food and feed safety standards in the UK are maintained.
The UK has one of the safest food systems in the world, and the agreement will maintain our ability to protect it by giving us access to information, expertise and cooperation.

From a food safety perspective, one of the biggest benefits is closer cooperation with European scientific and regulatory networks. This includes access to relevant EU agencies, systems and databases for food and feed safety. UK experts will be able to participate in agencies such as the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), contributing in the same way as Member State scientists. UK evidence will inform EU risk assessments.

Access to EU systems and databases, such as the interactive Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (iRASFF), will give us the latest information on emerging risks and help us trace and resolve problems faster, across the UK and the EU.
What should businesses do now?
Many businesses will see real benefits, but the impact will differ between sectors.

Even businesses that do not trade with the EU may need to make changes, because rules on food, agricultural goods, animal and plant health will need to align with EU rules. This may mean changing ingredients, recipes or labels, for example, and will affect businesses of all sizes, from bakeries and butchers to large retailers such as supermarkets.

Beth y dylai busnesau ei wneud nawr?
Bydd llawer o fusnesau’n gweld manteision, ond bydd yr effaith yn amrywio rhwng sectorau.

title: UK-EU SPS Agreement: what farmers and growers need to know

content.content: Today (Friday 20 November), at a summit in Brussels, the UK agreed a new Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreement with the European Union (EU).

For many businesses, the Agreement will make trade in plants, animals, food and related products between the UK and EU easier, cheaper and more predictable. It aims to reduce the paperwork, certification costs and border delays that can make trading with the EU difficult. It could add up to £5.1bn to the UK economy.
The Agreement will apply from 1 March 2028. Farms and businesses may need to make changes ahead of this date to prepare and make the most of the opportunities it presents.
In this post, we explain what the Agreement is, what this could mean for farmers and growers, how to prepare and where to get updates.
Overview

The UK and EU have agreed to align on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) rules covering food and feed, plants, animals and other agri-food goods. This alignment is intended to make trade with our biggest market cheaper and easier, cutting costs on red tape for British producers and retailers.
To support these trade opportunities, the Agreement will simplify the movement of goods between Great Britain and the EU. The main changes include:

But the Agreement is not just about imports and exports. It will also affect some of the rules that apply domestically. This means your farm or business could be affected even if you do not trade with the EU.
The Agreement includes a range of rules affecting farming and food production, including:
What this means for you
What these changes mean for your business will depend on what you produce, the products you use and where you trade.
For more information on the changes outlined below, read our updated guidance. It explains what the Agreement could mean for your sector and how you can start preparing for 1 March 2028.
More detailed guidance will be published for affected sectors throughout 2027.
If you trade with the EU

Importing and exporting agri-food goods between Great Britain and the EU will become simpler, with fewer routine checks and reduced paperwork and certification for some goods. This will be particularly beneficial for imports and exports of fresh or time-sensitive goods between the UK and the EU.
If you are an arable farmer or grower
Changes to rules on pesticides, pesticide residue limits and treated seed could affect crop protection choices and the treated seeds you can use.
If you keep livestock

Changes will affect animal identification, holding registration, animal movements and disease reporting, control and eradication programmes. They will affect the use of veterinary medicines, including antimicrobials, as well as feed additives, disinfectants and other products used on farms. We will retain our high animal welfare standards.
If you supply farms and food producers

You could be affected if you produce, process, supply or move goods used in farming and food supply chains. These include animals and animal products, plants and plant products, food, feed, pesticides, biocides and other inputs.
Businesses supplying the UK market and those trading with countries outside the EU may also be affected.

title: Exhibiting at the UK Chamber of Shipping's bi-annual conference

content.content: Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) colleagues exhibited for the first time at the UK Chamber of Shipping's bi-annual conference, held at the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in London. The event centred on the theme of 'Navigating the future' and explored the UK's role in shaping global maritime policy.

The UK Chamber of Shipping is the is the leading lobbying and representative body for the UK shipping sector. The event brings together industry stakeholders and UK policy makers to discuss the future of shipping. It also acts to promote the UK’s role in shaping global maritime policy and how the industry can work together to improve standards.

MCA teams in attendance were from The UK Ship Register (UKSR) and the UK Maritime Innovation Hub (UKMIH). The decision to exhibit this year was made due to wide scale updates within the agency, including the launch of the UKMIH in April 2026.
About the UK Ship Register
The UK Ship Register is a service provided by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) that allows individuals to register their vessels for use at sea.

Registering a vessel with the UK Ship Register means that it falls under the UK Flag. The UK Flag has a reputation for maintaining the highest international standards and is one of the best performing flags in the major Port State Control Schemes.
About the UK Maritime Innovation Hub

The UK Maritime Innovation Hub is a service of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), providing coordinated access to regulatory engagement for organisations developing innovative maritime technologies. Drawing on expertise from across the MCA, it supports clear, early and more structured engagement where this can add value, particularly in the areas of autonomy (MASS), decarbonisation (including energy efficiency and alternative fuels), digital systems and digitalisation technologies, and nuclear propulsion.

title: The Yerevan Pathway: COP17 aims to put the world on track for nature recovery

content.content: My name is David, and I’m the Chair of the Joint Nature Conservation Committee.
This post is a reflection on my time spent at the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.
A global plan  - but progress needed
After two weeks of intense negotiations, the conference concluded with agreement on the Yerevan Pathway – a shared plan to accelerate global action to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

This is an important achievement. Biodiversity underpins our food, water, health, economies and security. Its decline threatens livelihoods and prosperity, and increases vulnerability to extreme events.
But what encouraged me most was the determination of people from across the world to work together for nature, despite difficult geopolitical and economic circumstances.
Four years ago, in Montreal, governments adopted the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework: 23 targets for 2030 and four longer-term goals to halt and reverse nature loss.
COP17 marked the halfway point to 2030. The first global report of collective progress showed unprecedented engagement by countries, but also that we are not on track to achieve the agreed targets.
The global report drew on national reports that have been provided by over 170 countries. The UK’s own report on progress was coordinated by JNCC, drawing on the UK Biodiversity Indicators.

The Yerevan Pathway, adopted alongside some 40 other decisions, acknowledges this gap. It calls for accelerated implementation, stronger action across government and society, improved monitoring and increased resources, particularly for developing countries.
Tackling the causes of nature loss
The Pathway recognises that we must tackle the underlying drivers of biodiversity loss.
Conservation and restoration remain essential, but cannot succeed while economic systems continue to drive nature's decline.

Behind pressures such as land-use change, overexploitation, pollution, climate change and invasive species lie patterns of production and consumption, economic incentives, governance and societal values.

Reforming harmful subsidies and incentives is especially important. Under Target 18, countries agreed to reduce harmful incentives by at least $500 billion annually by 2030, while increasing positive incentives.

Progress has been slow, and negotiations in Yerevan were contentious. Nevertheless, the final agreement encourages accelerated implementation of Target 18. This issue was given further impetus by the COP Presidency, who announced one of many complementary initiatives on this topic.
Action and determination across society
COPs are much more than intergovernmental negotiations.
Beyond the negotiations, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women, young people, scientists, businesses and organisations demonstrated practical action and exchanged ideas.

I joined events run by youth networks, researchers and Indigenous organisations. I was struck by the passion of Indigenous Peoples and local communities defending their rights, territories and livelihoods, and by the commitment of young people. They are essential partners and leaders in nature recovery.

Discussions reinforced the importance of combining scientific evidence with Indigenous and local knowledge. For JNCC, providing robust evidence, monitoring progress and informing decisions are important contributions to this collective effort.
Mobilising finance and progress on the Cali Fund
Finance remained one of COP17's most difficult issues.
At various events throughout the conference, I saw growing recognition that nature recovery requires changes in how economies operate.
We must invest more in nature and stop financing its destruction.

Many developing countries face high debt, limited resources and declining aid, and we cannot yet show that the target of $20 billion annually in international biodiversity finance by 2025 has been achieved.

Nevertheless, there were positive developments. Countries made further pledges to various funds, and also agreed measures to improve access to finance and advance discussions on longer-term financial arrangements.

I was proud to see the UK playing a particularly constructive role, including the announcements of £20 million of new funding to protect coral reefs, marine wildlife and the coastal communities that depend on them, as well as its contributions to the Tropical Forests Forever Facility and the Global Environment Facility.
Another encouraging outcome concerned the Cali Fund, established at COP16 to share benefits from the use of digital sequence information on genetic resources.
Countries clarified arrangements for recognising companies' monetary contributions and agreed further work on the Fund's operation and distribution of benefits.

The Fund could generate substantial funding for biodiversity, including for Indigenous Peoples and local communities. Yet contributions remain tiny compared with its potential. The steps taken at COP17 could help turn an important innovation into a meaningful source of finance for nature.
We are making welcome progress, but overall funding for nature remains far below what is required.
Multilateralism prevails, but the real test begins at home
COP17 was far from perfect. Negotiations were sometimes frustrating, compromises weakened ambition and several issues remained unresolved.
Yet I left Yerevan encouraged.
I witnessed delegates with very different perspectives working tirelessly together to find common ground. I was proud to see the UK playing a particularly constructive role across many agenda items.
Equally inspiring was the determination of rights-holders and stakeholders to make their voices heard and contribute solutions.
At a time when international cooperation is under considerable strain, COP17 demonstrated that multilateralism still works – imperfectly and sometimes painfully slowly, but with real results.
And cooperation is indispensable. Nature loss crosses national borders; no country can reverse it alone.
The Yerevan Pathway provides renewed direction, but international agreements do not, by themselves, restore nature.

Governments must now translate commitments into stronger policies, budgets and investments, embedding nature across agriculture, fisheries, infrastructure, finance, trade and wider economic decision-making.

Nature must become central to all government departments, not remain the responsibility of environment ministries alone. Businesses, financial institutions and wider society must also play their part.
The determination I witnessed in Yerevan gives me hope. We have a shared global plan, a renewed pathway and growing evidence of what needs to change.
Now we must turn that determination into action - so that by 2030, nature is genuinely on the path to recovery, for the benefit of nature, people and the planet.

description: David Cooper is Chair of the UK’s Joint Nature Conservation Committee (the UK’s statutory nature advisor). In our final post about COP17, David reflects on his time in Armenia at the conference.

title: How to protect your school’s money from fraud
authors: Soleil Buttle, Department for Education, Senior Counter Fraud Officer

content.content: Soleil Buttle, Senior Counter Fraud Officer at the Department for Education (DfE) explains how recognising the signs of fraud and taking practical steps to reduce risk can help education settings protect their funding.
Here are five quick checks you can use today. They only take a few minutes, and can help protect your school’s money, time and resources.
If you look after money, suppliers, payroll or grants in a school or academy trust, I encourage you to read this.
You already do a lot to look after your school's money. I want to help with one part of that: spotting the signs of fraud by knowing what to look out for.
Why this matters to your school

Every pound in your budget is an investment in your pupils. Fraud takes that money away. If a payment goes to the wrong account, you may spend days talking to your bank, your supplier and your trust. Checking first takes minutes.

During 2023 to 2024*, DfE helped stop over £104 million of fraud. We detected more than £12 million of fraud and recovered more than £66 million linked to fraud and error. Every pound protected from fraud is money that can continue to support learners.
Where fraud is identified in schools
Fraudsters create urgency. They may urge or pressure you to pay an invoice or take action quickly, hoping you’ll respond before you have time to stop and check.
Common risks include:
Five checks you can use today

Fraud can happen to anyone. Fraudsters deliberately make their approaches convincing. If something doesn’t feel right, speak up as soon as you can. Reporting your concerns can help protect your school and others too.
Invoice fraud

Invoice fraud is one scam to look out for. It often starts with an email that looks like it's from a supplier you know. It asks you to change their bank details. The email may look just like the real thing.

We worked with the National Crime Agency (NCA) to write a short leaflet on how to spot it. It explains the warning signs and what to do. It's a quick read, and it could save your school a lot of money.
Free help
If you spot something, tell us. We can only build a clear picture of what's happening if schools and trusts report it.
You can email your concern to allegations.mailbox@education.gov.uk. Try to include:
We won't share who you are without your permission unless the law says we must. If you report anonymously, we may not be able to investigate.
We have free help for you and your team:

International Fraud Awareness Week runs from 15 to 21 November 2026. It's a good moment to talk about fraud with your team. But fraud doesn't stop when the week does, it’s important to stay vigilant all year.
What to do next
Sign up for DfE fraud news and alerts
It's free, and it takes about a minute. Share what you learn about preventing fraud with colleagues in finance, procurement, HR and IT.
As fraud tactics evolve, our defences must evolve with it.
Stay alert. Pause and check. Share what you learn. If something does not look right, report it.

title: Every Voice, Every Choice: Reflecting on Safeguarding Adults Week

content.content: As Safeguarding Adults Week draws to a close, we have been reflecting on the powerful contributions shared throughout the week and what they tell us about safeguarding at its best.

This year’s theme, “Every Voice. Every Choice”, has focused on the importance of meaningful co-production, Making Safeguarding Personal and ensuring that people have genuine voice and choice in decisions about their lives.

Though every person who contributed to our National Adult Safeguarding Week blogs approached safeguarding from very different places, a clear message connects them: good safeguarding starts with the person.
Listening, Choice and Curiosity

Lucy Rush opened the week with a deeply personal reflection on listening and communication. Through the experience of her Uncle Pete, she reminds us that losing the ability to speak does not mean losing your voice, your identity or your right to be heard. Her blog challenges us to recognise all the ways in which people communicate and to make listening an intervention in its own right.

Dr Clenton Farquharson CBE then reminded us that co-production must go beyond being invited into a conversation: People need real influence over decisions so they can live the lives they want. Success should be judged not simply by whether a safeguarding process has been completed, but by whether somebody feels safer, retains the relationships that matter to them and has greater control over their life.

Tamara Cooper brought another important perspective through her reflections on professional curiosity. Her powerful examples demonstrate why practitioners must be prepared to look beyond what appears obvious, suspend judgement and take the time to see and hear the person in front of them. Sometimes, one professional asking another question or staying a little longer can make an enormous difference.

Finally, Professor Michael Preston-Shoot asked us to think about how we turn learning into lasting change. We have a wealth of evidence from people with lived experience, practitioners, Safeguarding Adult Reviews, research and assurance activity; the challenge is ensuring that this learning shapes practice, services, governance and national policy.
Turning Learning into Action

Learning from evidence and experience is also central to the work of the National Adult Safeguarding Board, which Sarah is privileged to chair. Established in June 2026, the Board brings together people with lived experience, sector leaders and safeguarding professionals to strengthen national leadership, accountability, learning and improvement.

The Board is already beginning to translate learning into action by using evidence and recommendations to inform and co-produce revisions to the Care and Support Statutory Guidance - particularly, Chapter 14 on safeguarding - and will subsequently contribute to the review of legislation.
Reflecting on What Comes Next
For both of us, that connection between voice, learning and action is one of the most important messages to take from this week.

Safeguarding is not something we do to people. It must be something we do with them. That means listening differently, sharing power, remaining curious and being prepared to change our practice and systems in response to what we hear.

Safeguarding Adults Week gives us an important opportunity to pause and reflect on how we can empower every voice, but that principle needs to guide us throughout the year. Our task now is to turn these insights into consistent practice, so that every person can have meaningful choice in the decisions that affect their life.

We want to thank National Adult Safeguarding Board members – Lucy Rush, Dr Clenton Farquharson CBE, Tamara Cooper and Professor Michael Preston-Shoot – for sharing their experiences and expertise and challenging us all this week.

title: News coverage: landmark reforms to end the leasehold system

content.content: There has been widespread media coverage across print, broadcast and digital channels following MHCLG’s announcement on the introduction of the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill in Parliament, which will deliver some of the biggest changes to property law in more than a century.

Following an interview with the Housing Minister, The Guardian, reports that leaseholders in England and Wales will have ground rents capped at £250 a year in 2028. The paper describes the Bill as the biggest step yet towards ending the leasehold system, with Minister Pennycook calling the reforms a “historic moment” and the “beginning of the end for the feudal leasehold system”.

BBC News covered the announcement for online and broadcast, setting out the Bill measures and experiences of leaseholders. A clip of the Secretary of State featured in the package, setting out that “this legislation is very complex and that's why we've taken our time”. An explainer video also ran across the BBC’s social media channels, breaking down the changes simply to audiences.

The I Paper features an explainer on the difference between leasehold and commonhold. The Independent runs a positive piece focusing on the benefits the new Bill will bring to the lives of leaseholders calling it the “biggest shake up to the rules in a century”. The Times, Money Saving Expert, Financial Times and Metro also report positively on the reforms.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook was interviewed across national breakfast broadcast programmes, speaking to Times Radio, Sky News, BBC Breakfast, Bauer, Good Morning Britain, ITN, GB News and LBC. He also featured on BBC Radio 4’s evening programme where he described the bill as “laying the foundation for a commonhold future”.
The news was further picked up across national and regional radio bulletins, including BBC Radio 5, BBC Berkshire, BBC Suffolk, Times Radio and LBC News.

The announcement has received further coverage across trade and regional press. Devon Livereports that “thousands” of residents in Devon could benefit from the reforms, while the Manchester Evening News describes the Bill as a “major leasehold shake-up”. The Evening Standard highlights the impact the reforms could have in London where ‘one in three homes are leasehold’. Trade outlets also explore the impact on the sector, including Inside Housing, Housing Today, Property 118 and Property Industry Eye.
Across social media, explainer videos from BBC News, ITV News and BBC London set out the key reforms and the experience of leaseholders.

title: Making kindness part of school life

content.content: Every child deserves to feel safe, happy, and accepted at school, with trusted adults around them and a sense of belonging. Preventing bullying means more than having policies and procedures: it means making kindness, respect, and positive relationships part of everyday life. These grow through small moments, created by design rather than chance.
We are proud to support Anti-Bullying Week, but our commitment goes beyond one week. Our approach is proactive, building positive relationships from the start.
Building the foundations

Our pastoral and welfare provision helps children feel safe, valued, and heard. Through our wellbeing programme, they learn about their brains, recognise stress, manage emotions, and respond rather than react. Mindfulness and emotional regulation help build resilience and strategies for everyday worries.

One of our other programmes helps children across all year groups understand personal boundaries, recognise inappropriate behaviour, and seek help. For your school, you could start by reviewing how you teach emotional regulation and help-seeking: can children name a trusted adult and explain how to ask for support?
Making kindness everyone's responsibility

Our character curriculum encourages children to be upstanders: noticing when someone feels left out, offering support, and helping everyone feel welcome. Staff model positive relationships, celebrate differences, and reinforce empathy and fairness.

Pupil leadership puts this into practice. In KS1, Mini Police activities with our local PCSO build community connections. In KS2, Young Citizens undertake community projects, developing fairness and moral purpose. Play Leaders organise games and help others feel included.

Assemblies and classroom conversations celebrate kindness. To make this practical in your school, you could agree a consistent approach across staff to supporting children who are being left out of friendships or activities. Give pupils opportunities to lead activities that help others feel included and recognise everyday examples of kindness.
Listening and addressing concerns early

Children need to know someone will listen. Class-based Worry Monster boxes let them share concerns anonymously or by name. Welfare team drop-ins in our “Butterfly Room” offer space to talk, while mindfulness and self-regulation areas help children manage emotions and access support.

We investigate and follow up all reported concerns, with individual support where needed. I would recommend reviewing your own reporting routes with pupils: do they know where to go, who will listen, and what happens next? Make follow-up part of the response, not an afterthought.
Working in partnership with families

Strong family relationships help us identify difficulties early. Staff and leaders, visible in high-visibility jackets at the start of the day, make conversations easier. If this is something you have found a block in the past, then I’d consider how your school offers regular, approachable opportunities for parents to talk, before concerns escalate.
Tackling bullying is a shared responsibility: children need confidence to speak up, staff must remain vigilant, and parents must know we will listen and respond.
Wellbeing, belonging, and attendance

Children who feel anxious, isolated, or unsafe may become reluctant to attend. When attendance concerns arise, make space to ask about friendships, worries, and belonging, alongside other difficulties. We then use those conversations to identify support that helps children feel secure and ready to learn.
Consistency is key

The best place to start is by choosing one practical step to strengthen this term: review reporting routes, agree consistent adult responses, or widen pupil leadership. Build it into everyday routines rather than treating it as a one-off activity.
Ultimately, we want every child to know they matter and belong. When kindness, respect and inclusion shape school life, children can feel safe, flourish, and succeed.

description: Louise Smith, CEO at Warrington Primary Academy Trust, shares how schools can make kindness part of everyday life to strengthen pupil belonging and school culture.

title: Building stronger relationships with the fishing industry

content.content: The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) is committed to working closely with fishermen and the wider fishing industry to improve safety at sea.

We have been engaging with Regional Fisheries Groups (RFGs) and safety committees across England, creating opportunities for open conversations about the issues that matter most to those working in the sector.

These forums help us better understand the challenges faced by fishermen, while giving industry a stronger voice in shaping safety initiatives, guidance and future policy. They enable us to build collaborative and trusted relationships, ensuring that the expertise and experience within the fishing community is reflected in the work we do.
Listening and taking action

During 2026, MCA representatives attended Regional Fisheries Group meetings in ports across England, alongside colleagues from the Marine Management Organisation (MMO). The discussions provided valuable insights into the everyday challenges faced by fishermen, and potential areas for enhanced support from the MCA such as surveys, business practicalities and regulatory requirements.
While meaningful change takes time, our response is already underway and will continue over the coming months and years.
Making guidance easier to understand
We are reviewing other processes highlighted through the Regional Fisheries Groups, including vessel registration, changes of ownership and the application of fishing vessel Codes of Practice.
Shaping the future of fishing safety
The discussions taking place through the Regional Fisheries Groups are contributing to a wider conversation about the future of fishing safety.

The MCA has worked for many years with fishing federations and industry partners on strategies aimed at reducing fatalities and serious incidents, particularly those related to man-overboard incidents, vessel stability and accidents to crew members.

The current Home and Dry Group Fishing Safety Strategy concludes in 2027. As work begins on the next strategy, we believe the industry itself should play a leading role in shaping its priorities and direction. Those working at sea every day have the knowledge and experience needed to identify what works, where improvements are needed and how safety can be strengthened across the sector.
For that reason, we have invited industry federations to take a leading role in developing the next five-year Home and Dry Group Fishing Safety Strategy.
Continuing the conversation
We are committed to listening, learning and acting where improvements can be made.

Not every concern raised will have an immediate solution, and there will be occasions where changes are not possible. However, we are committed to being open about our decisions and keeping the industry informed about the progress being made.

We look forward to continuing these conversations through the Regional Fisheries Groups and meeting fishermen across the country in the coming months. By listening to the industry and working together, we can help build a safer and more collaborative future for fishing.

We welcome feedback from across the fishing industry and are committed to working openly and constructively with fishermen and their representative federations. We are aware of the NFFO, SFF and NIFF survey seeking views and experiences of the MCA and welcome the opportunity to hear directly from the industry. We will listen carefully to the feedback and continue working with the federations to understand where improvements can be made.
If you have ideas about how we can improve our engagement, we would also like to hear from you directly. Please contact us at fishing@mcga.gov.uk.

title: How does Defra know it's making a difference

content.content: What we did

We found that people care deeply about delivering positive outcomes. But our research suggests we find it easier to explain what we are delivering rather than how it contributes to the change we want to see.

We gathered evidence from user research and conversations about outcomes, service performance, and service ownership. We spoke to people working in a range of roles across Defra group and its arm's length bodies. We wanted to understand what helps, and what gets in the way of Defra becoming more outcome focused.
As part of the research, we asked colleagues to describe what an outcome is. Their answers really made us think.

The term can sometimes feel abstract, strategic, or disconnected from day-to-day work. Yet, outcomes are at the heart of what Defra exists to do. Outcomes are the changes Defra wants to achieve for people, nature and the environment. They support Defra’s vision to restore nature, support growth, and improve security.
The ‘golden thread’

One theme ran throughout the research: important parts of the system are not always connected in useful ways. We need a better understanding of whether the things we’re doing actually help achieve the change we want in the world. This includes being clearer about the outcomes we're aiming for, introducing new ownership models, improving how we measure performance, and providing better tools to help generate insights to inform decisions. These elements exist, but the connections between them are often fragmented. As one research participant noted:

Defra is a ministerial department supported by 34 agencies and public bodies operating in a complex ecosystem. The problem is not the work itself. It’s that the connections between different areas of work can be weak or difficult to see.
Some of the challenges are below the surface

Reporting burdens, disconnected data, unclear accountability and duplicated work are easy to see. But participants pointed to deeper root causes, including governance, funding, organisational structures, ownership and culture.

Improving dashboards, reports, or evidence measures alone will not solve the underlying problem. Lasting change may depend just as much on shared understanding, trust, collaboration and decision-making as it does on new tools or processes.
We don't all mean the same thing
Another strong theme was that people spend a lot of time trying to understand each other’s language.
Teams use words such as outcomes, services, performance and transformation in different ways. Sometimes we need to agree definitions before we can discuss the work itself.

When teams have different views of what a service is, or what success looks like, it becomes harder to collaborate, share evidence, prioritise and make investment decisions. Differences in language can reveal something deeper: a lack of shared understanding about how Defra achieves its outcomes.
We're rich in data, but insight is harder
Information is spread across teams, systems and organisations. People must often find, check, combine and interpret it before they can use it.
Many people also feel that measurement focuses more on activity than outcomes.
It is usually easier to count transactions, milestones, and tasks completed than to understand whether they have led to meaningful change. As one research participant put it:

Better insight does not always mean collecting more data. It means connecting the information we already have so people can understand how well we are achieving our outcomes and learn what works. Better insight can also help Defra make more informed investment decisions.
Reasons to be optimistic
While the findings are challenging, they are also encouraging.
Our research found growing enthusiasm for outcome-focused and service-led working. Participants valued evidence and insight, and many felt that the foundations for change already exist.

Research participants described a future where outcomes, services, performance and decision-making are connected through a much stronger 'golden thread'. In this future, Defra will use evidence and insight in a better way, to evidence what we did, assess the difference it made, and decide what to do next.
Work is already happening across Defra to make these connections stronger. For me, that was the most encouraging finding.
What’s next

We’re now starting part one of our test-and-learn experiment, focussing on Waste as our first outcome area. We're beginning conversations with people working across Waste to understand how outcomes, policy, services, evidence and decision-making currently connect, and where the golden thread is strong or breaks down.

This will give us a clearer picture of how the system works today and what we might test next to strengthen those connections. Early in the new year, we’ll share another blog about our plans for the experiment and what we’re starting to learn.
More information

Amy Wilson is a senior user researcher in Defra Digital Data Technology and Security. Get in touch with amy.wilson@defra.gov.uk to find out more, share evidence or tell us about similar work elsewhere in government.

If you're interested in finding out more about what we do in Defra Digital Data Technology and Security check out our LinkedIn page for all the latest news, stories and job openings. While you're there, why not give us a follow?

title: 5 reasons to vaccinate your 2- or 3-year-old against flu

content.content: Many of us think of flu as being a bad cold, but it is an unpleasant illness that can be life-threatening for some. Under- 5s are the group of children at the greatest risk of experiencing serious flu complications, as their airways are narrower and their immune systems are still developing. Most children recover from flu within a week and are well enough to go back to nursery or school, but some are hospitalised and have a slower recovery.

All children who were aged 2 or 3 years old on 31 August 2026 are eligible for the free flu vaccine this year, given as a nasal spray. If you have a child of this age, you should have already received an invitation for them to be vaccinated at their GP practice. You can also contact your GP practice to book an appointment, and some pharmacies can also vaccinate children of this age.
Here are 5 reasons to have your 2- or 3-year-old vaccinated against flu

Children under 5 have the highest hospitalisation rate due to flu. Vaccination cuts the hospitalisation risk by around two-thirds. It also helps protect against complications like pneumonia and painful ear infections.
2. Protect family and friends

Pre-schoolers can pick up illnesses more easily than others. Vaccinating your child helps reduce the chance of others in your family who are higher risk, like grandparents or those with long-term conditions, getting flu.
3. No needles

The nasal spray is painless and easy to have. It contains weakened flu viruses to help your child build immunity and fight off flu. The vaccine is absorbed into the nose really quickly, so even if your child sneezes right after, it still works. Parents who do not wish for their child to have the nasal spray version of the vaccine, or whose children can't have the nasal spray for medical reasons, can ask their GP practice for an alternative flu vaccine injection.
4. It’s safe and works really well

The nasal spray helps protect against flu, has been given to millions of children in the UK and worldwide, and has an excellent safety record. The vaccine is updated yearly to match flu strains, so we recommend vaccinating yearly, even if vaccinated last year.
5. Avoid disruption

Getting vaccinated reduces your child’s risk of catching, or being seriously unwell, with flu, which can mean time off nursery or pre-school. If your child gets flu, you may have to take time off or find childcare.
Get ready for winter, by booking in your 2- or 3-year-old with your GP practice or at your local pharmacy.

title: CLA conference: supporting farm growth and resilience

content.content: Today, Secretary of State Dame Angela Eagle addressed the Country Land and Business Association (CLA) Rural Business Conference.

In her speech, the Secretary of State announced a package of measures that will help support growth in rural postcodes and put agricultural at the heart of our economy, security, and national identity.
The package included measures to help farm businesses in England invest, grow and become more resilient.
This post brings together the main updates, including support for on-farm reservoirs, work to help farmers access private investment, and an update on Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT).
Growth
Funding for soil and water innovation
The Farming Innovation Programme (FIP) ‘Healthy Soils and Water for a Sustainable Environment’ competition’ opened for applications today (19 November 2026).

Up to £28 million is available for innovative projects to improve soil health, water quality and environmental management in livestock and cropping systems on farms in England. This is the largest FIP competition since it launched in October 2021.

This funding will give farmers and rural businesses across the country the tools to become more productive and resilient, while creating opportunities for innovative businesses and technologies to grow.
Read our dedicated Farming Blog post for more information about the competition and where to find application guidance.
Rural communities

Rural areas make up over 85% of England’s land mass. Rural England is home to 9.7 million people (17% of the population in 2024), and rural areas contributed over £259 billion (12%) to the economy in England in 2023.

Thriving rural communities and a prosperous rural economy will be underpinned by improvements in rural connectivity (transport and digital), availability of affordable housing and energy, and access to a range of community services.

In July, we published the Future of Rural England report, which includes practical recommendations to place rural communities at the heart of government decision-making. The report builds on the work of the Defra-led Rural Taskforce, working across Whitehall and with external partners to support rural businesses and tackle rural disadvantage.

The report confirmed plans for a cross-government rural proofing board so rural needs are considered as policy is developed. Annual reporting will make it clearer how departments are delivering for rural England.
Farmer Collaboration Fund

The Farmer Collaboration Fund helps farmers and land managers work together on local projects to improve productivity, sustainability and resilience. It funds organisations that support new and existing clusters and collaboration groups.

We received a high number of applications for Round one of the fund and are assessing them. Successful applicants will be notified soon. We'll publish the list of recipients on the blog in due course.
Read more about how the Farmer Collaboration Fund supports farmers working together.
Nature markets

We’ve set up the Farming Profitability and Private Finance Taskforce to help farmers access private investment. It will focus on practical opportunities to support more productive, resilient and sustainable farming systems.
We’re delighted that Lloyds Banking Group will support Defra in co-chairing the taskforce.

Our recent publication, Growing Places, sets out how we are working to help connect private finance with the needs and opportunities presented by nature markets for healthier, more resilient places. This includes, for the first time, proposing principles for combining public and private environmental payments.
We want your views to help shape these principles. You can contact Defra at naturemarkets@defra.gov.uk or register for upcoming webinars on combining public and private environmental payments:

You only need to register for one webinar. Both webinars will  cover the same content: background to the principles proposed in Growing Places. There will be an opportunity to ask questions live and you can also pre-submit them when you sign up for the events.
A long-term vision for the tenanted sector

Defra is inviting the tenanted sector to work with us to develop a shared plan to build a resilient, profitable and productive tenanted sector, as part of the next step to deliver the Farming Roadmap.

We want to build a tenanted sector where tenants have confidence to invest and grow their businesses and landlords have confidence to let land and invest in their tenanted holdings. Supporting existing tenants and new entrants.
Over the coming months, we'll work with industry representatives – including the CLA, TFA, NFU and professional bodies - to set up workshops with tenants, landlords and advisors to gather views.
Anyone interested in getting involved can contact Defra at agriculturaltenancies@defra.gov.uk and we will be in touch with a list of engagement opportunities in due course.
You can read more about our plans to develop a vision for the tenanted sector in this blog post.
Resilience

Helping farms grow also means helping them prepare for drought and build businesses that can withstand the impacts of geopolitical shocks and a changing climate. These updates cover water management, environmental land management, fertiliser supplies and food production.
Fertiliser supplies and resilience
The UK remains reliant on imports for our fertiliser supplies, making our farming sector vulnerable to global market disruptions and price fluctuations.

We’ve published a short paper today which sets out our initial plans for developing a Fertiliser Sustainability and Resilience Plan for England. We are inviting stakeholders to contribute ahead of a full plan to be published in the spring.

The aim is to boost the UKs fertiliser supply resilience, identify areas where we can take a more holistic approach to nutrient management, and reduce reliance on imports. We are wanting to set out a longer-term plan to start this transition, aligned with our farming roadmap commitments, water regulations and circular economy goals.
Water management and on-farm reservoirs

Today (19 November) we've published the guidance for round 3 of the Water Management Grant, which will provide up to £15 million to support on-farm reservoirs and water tanks. Guidance and eligibility criteria have been published.
The application window will open on 30 November 2026 and will close on 23 February at 11:59pm.
This is a competitive grant scheme, and applications are not prioritised based on when they are submitted. Take the time you need to prepare your application before submitting it.

Read our dedicated Farming Blog post for more information about the grant, the published guidance, a webinar for those considering applying and the steps government is taking to make it easier to build and use reservoirs.
Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI)
We know the high demand for the SFI has raised concerns about access to funding.
Defra is working at pace to improve SFI for next year – continuing our close work with farmers and stakeholders by listening to experiences and learning lessons from this window.
Ministers have confirmed we will move away from a first come first served application process for SFI in 2027. We are exploring alternatives as part of this engagement with the sector.
We’re also looking at how we can give farmers clear guidance and support, so they have plenty of time to get ready to apply.
We will provide further details on the future of SFI in due course.
The RPA continue to issue agreement offers to those who applied for SFI26. As of 18 November:
We’re also confirming today that we’ve increased payment rates for moorland actions in SFI24, aligning with equivalent rates in the SFI26 offer. More information can be found below.
Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT)
We’ve recently made several improvements to CSHT to give more farmers access to funding.
Commons Trial

We’ve started a trial for a small number of commoners to test the new application approach and digital service. The selected commons have been working with advisers from Natural England and the Forestry Commission to finalise their applications.
We’ll provide an update on the progress of the trial in early January, and subject to its success, an update on when we expect the wider rollout to commence.
Increasing moorland payment rates

We’ve increased payment rates for a select number of moorland actions, as confirmed in previous blogs. This aligns equivalent SFI24 and CSHT actions (for agreements that started in 2025), with rates in the SFI26 offer.
This ensures those farming above the moorland line are properly compensated for the action they’re taking to improve the condition of moorland habitats.
Letters have now been sent to all affected agreement holders outlining the changes.

The increases will apply to existing SFI24 agreements and new and existing CSHT agreements. Payments will be backdated to the start of each agreement. Farmers do not need to take any action; current and future payments will be adjusted automatically.
Details of the payment rate increases can be seen below.

CSHT actions:
Single-focus agreements

Earlier this month, we opened expressions of interest for two new single-focus agreements covering traditional orchards and wet grassland for wintering waders and wildfowl. These simplified agreements focus on delivering priority environmental actions.
They build on the single-focus agreements introduced in July for species-rich grassland and scheduled monument management, which remain open for expressions of interest.
Read our blog post on new CSHT single-focus agreements for eligibility restrictions, how to express an interest and seasonal survey requirements for species-rich grassland.

title: From Learning to Action: Strengthening Adult Safeguarding

content.content: From Learning to Action - Blog by Professor Michael Preston-Shoot

The establishment of the National Adult Safeguarding Board (NASB) is a milestone in the development of adult safeguarding law and policy. It represents a significant opportunity to strengthen accountability at all governance, policy and practice levels. It also represents a significant opportunity to collate learning about the effectiveness of adult safeguarding law, policy and practice. As Stephen Kinnock, then Minister of State for Social Care, said in his introductory remarks at the inaugural NASB meeting, we all have a responsibility to listen, to hear and then to act.

We have no shortage of learning about what is working well in adult safeguarding and where there continue to be shortcomings. It comes from people with lived experience of adult safeguarding, and from practitioners who have had the privilege to work with them. It comes from two national analyses of safeguarding adult reviews, Care Quality Commission assessment of local authority safeguarding outcomes, and from research and briefings published by Research in Practice, the Local Government Association, and the National Network for Safeguarding Adult Board Chairs.

Collating this learning directs reflection across five domains: direct practice with individuals at risk of, or experiencing abuse and neglect, inter-agency collaboration and co-operation, organisational support for practice and service development, governance, and the national context. This learning encourages reflection not just on the evidence of good practice and shortcomings in each of the five domains, but also on the degree to which there is or is not alignment across the domains. In other words, is what is happening in one domain supporting or hindering work in another domain?

The NASB has already begun to lead on, and oversee projects that are designed to translate learning and reflection into change. Most notably, findings and recommendations from the aforesaid learning will be used to inform and to co-produce revisions to the Care and Support Statutory Guidance, especially chapter 14 on safeguarding, and subsequently to contribute to the review of legislation.

However, learning and reflection as a precursor to change is not just an NASB responsibility. It is a key responsibility of Safeguarding Adults Board, with their mandate to seek assurance about the effectiveness of adult safeguarding, to collate outcomes from reviews and audits, and to action plan where shortcomings are found. Learning and reflection for change is also a responsibility for commissioners and providers, working together and with people with lived experience of service provision, to strengthen provision where it is working well and to remedy gaps where these are found.

Learning and reflection for change must also be a central thread of every multi-agency meeting where risk is a key concern. It involves drawing on knowledge and experience of adult safeguarding, including legal literacy, and sharing this not just with colleagues across health, housing, social care, uniform services and others, but crucially also with those individuals at the centre of our work and, where appropriate with their families, friends and advocates. This is the link to making safeguarding personal and to giving meaning to the six principles of adult safeguarding in work with individuals at risk of, or experiencing abuse and neglect.

Adult safeguarding week should not be the only time where all of us involved in adult safeguarding reflect on what we have learned and what we should take from that learning into our contributions to practice, the management of practice, service development and/or policy review. However, it is a week where for a time all of us can step back, pause, take stock and refresh in order to continue our human work with determination, compassion, openness and commitment.

title: From roads to rivers: what does runoff mean for our waters?

content.content: Road runoff can carry a mix of particles and chemicals into our water. Some of these are known to pose a risk to wildlife, while the risks from others are less well understood. New Environment Agency research is helping to build a clearer picture to help prioritise the action we and other organisations can take to manage and improve water quality.
What is runoff?

When it rains, water runs off roads, roofs and other hard surfaces, carrying with it a mixture of contaminants. This includes particles and chemicals that have built up on road and urban surfaces from various sources, such as vehicles, the road surface itself, or deposited from the air. These contaminants can be washed into nearby water environments, where some may affect water quality and aquatic life, depending on the substance and its concentration.
Surface runoff is part of everyday life but how significant is this problem?
What does Environment Agency research show about road runoff?

At the Environment Agency, we are working to build a clearer picture of the impact that road runoff has on our rivers and lakes. Our scientists have recently reviewed hundreds of scientific studies on road runoff. This includes research on modelling pollution and the effectiveness of treatment methods. We also considered how pollution from roads might change in the future with climate change and the transition to electric vehicles.

Highway and urban runoff is not a single, simple issue. It is made up of a mixture of pollutants. This includes well-studied substances such as metals and oil-related chemicals, as well as newer concerns such as microplastics, substances used in tyre production and persistent chemicals like PFAS, often referred to as ‘forever chemicals’.

There is growing scientific interest in how these substances behave once they enter rivers. For example, research in the United States has linked a chemical found in tyres to the death of Pacific coho salmon when it is washed into waterways during rainfall. While we do not have evidence of the same effect occurring in England, studies like this highlight why it is important to understand what is present in runoff and how it might affect wildlife under different conditions.

This matters because pollutants do not enter the environment in isolation. They arrive together, and their combined effects on wildlife are not yet fully understood. Our evidence review also shows that the scale and type of pollution vary depending on traffic, land use, infrastructure and weather. Urban areas are likely to be hotspots of pollution in runoff because of the extent of hard surfaces and factors like driving patterns.

While this work highlights some important gaps, it provides a much clearer foundation than before. It allows us to focus future research, improve how we assess risk, and provide more informed advice to those responsible for managing roads and drainage.
What we know about vehicle tyre wear pollution

Tyre wear is part of this wider picture. As vehicles travel, friction between tyres and the road surface produces very small particles, known as tyre wear particles. These contribute significantly to microplastics in the environment and can contain a range of associated chemicals used in tyre manufacture.

To help us understand this issue better, our scientists have developed a model to estimate the release of tyre wear particles and associated chemicals into the environment on a local and national scale. The model can be adjusted to account for different assumptions about traffic, conditions and location. It provides an important starting point for the Environment Agency and our partners.

This modelling approach is valuable because it can be used to identify areas where releases are likely to be higher, allowing effort to be targeted where it will have the greatest benefit. By making this approach available, we can support others in taking more informed and targeted action. Put simply, it gives us a way to begin addressing an issue that would otherwise be difficult to quantify.
How can road runoff pollution be tackled?
Improving our understanding of road runoff supports practical measures to reduce its impact.

We are working with National Highways to tackle pollution from motorways and major A roads across England, by helping to identify where improvements are needed at the highest risk locations. New or upgraded water treatment systems and nature-based solutions are being designed to capture sediment and reduce the amount of pollution entering rivers.
We are also working with Loughborough University and others to better understand the impacts of tyre wear particles on humans and our environment, and how we can engineer solutions to reduce this.
The journey ahead

Tackling pollution from roads is a complex challenge – it will require a combination of better evidence, targeted investment, and continued collaboration between organisations responsible for roads, water and the environment.
To explore the science behind this work and what it means for our environment, read the full reports on GOV.UK:

title: From Evidence to Action: Highlights from the One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Conference

content.content: World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW), 18 – 24 November, is a global campaign that takes place annually, to improve awareness and understanding of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) and encourage best practices among the public, One Health stakeholders and policymakers, who all play a critical role in reducing the further emergence and spread of AMR. Under Cefas’ role as part of the UK’s FAO Reference Centre for AMR, WAAW provides an opportunity to raise awareness of the threat and solutions to tackle AMR.

Antimicrobial resistance, or AMR, happens when bacteria and other microbes no longer respond to the medicines designed to treat them. It is a global health threat, with significant implications for people, animals, food systems and the environment. That is why tackling AMR needs a One Health approach, bringing together expertise from human health, animal health, food production and environmental sectors.

In February 2026, 131 delegates from 29 countries came together in Bangkok, Thailand, for a regional South and Southeast Asia One Health AMR Conference. The event brought together representatives from governments, academia, industry, NGOs and other FAO Reference Centres for AMR, with more than 35 speakers contributing perspectives from across the globe.

The conference featured contributions from internationally recognised leaders and AMR practitioners from Asia and beyond. The programme was designed to move beyond discussion of the problem and focus on how evidence can be turned into action. Across the 2.5 days, the agenda followed a clear journey: from global AMR governance and regional surveillance, through case studies in AMR and AMU, to data sharing, policy, innovation, economics and long-term sustainability. The presentations and panel discussions showcased recent AMR successes, including those supported by the Fleming Fund, and highlighted the importance of translating AMR data into action. Sessions also explored regional efforts focusing on reducing AMU in terrestrial and aquatic animals; veterinary medicines residues in foods of animal origin; AMR in bacterial pathogens with zoonotic potential; and economic insights on AMR. Interactive sessions were used throughout the programme to capture audience views and reflections, giving delegates a chance to share experiences, challenges and priorities in real time.

Interactive sessions were used throughout the programme to capture audience views and reflections, giving delegates a chance to share experiences, challenges and priorities in real time.

Professor Rungtip Chuanchuen of the Faculty of Veterinary Science, Chulalongkorn University set the scene with a keynote talk exploring how a One Health approach can help address AMR across agri-food systems. Dame Sally Davies, the UK’s Special Envoy on AMR, provided an inspiring opening address that underscored the need for global cooperation and continued action. Looking to the future, Jorge Martin-Almagro, UK’s Defra Deputy Chief Veterinary Officer, chaired discussions on sustainability and joined the closing session, highlighting the importance of maintaining momentum and ensuring long-term impact from AMR surveillance and control programmes.

A highlight of the conference was the Future AMR Leader Perspectives session included contributions from Fleming Fund Fellows from Africa and Asia. Talks covered topics on AMR in food animals, the cost of One Health AMR National Action Plans, using animal health data for policy action, and operationalising AMR surveillance in lower-resource settings. Another highlight was the AMR Community of Practice session, which focused on connecting people, celebrating impact and driving One Health solutions to AMR. The session included a presentation on what the Community of Practice has achieved, certificate presentation and an interactive activity for participants. This was an important reminder that networks and relationships are central to sustaining AMR work after formal projects or funding cycles end.

The conference outcomes focused on strengthening collaboration, improving surveillance and data sharing, identifying sustainable approaches, developing actionable recommendations, and supporting policy and regulatory progress.

Athina Papadopoulou, Cefas, commented, "The conference was a great success, bringing together participants from 29 countries around the world. The level of engagement was exceptional; attendees were open in sharing their experiences, but also challenges, and genuinely committed to collaboration. It has been incredibly rewarding to see such a positive outcome after 18 months of preparation. The event provided a valuable opportunity to meet new collaborators and hold meetings with existing regional partners and discuss plans on upcoming projects with new ones. I am confident that the conversations and connections established here will lead to new opportunities in the coming months."

Claire Gilbert, the Veterinary Medicines Directorate (VMD), added, “The event provided an excellent opportunity to network, meet new potential partners, and explore opportunities for future collaboration. It was fantastic to hear a range of perspectives and learn from the innovative ideas and experiences being shared from across the region. The connections made during the conference have already started to lead to the development of new partnerships and projects.”

The event was organised by the UK’s FAO designated Reference Centre for AMR, together with partners from FAO Reference Centre for AMR, Chulalongkorn University, FDA Thailand, Department of Livestock Development in Thailand, Mott MacDonald, the National Parks Board of Singapore, and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific. The UK FAO Reference Centre for AMR is a shared designation with the UK’s Animal and Plant Health Agency, Cefas and the Veterinary Medicines Directorate. These agencies combine their expertise to support partners Low- and Middle-income countries to strengthen AMR surveillance and antimicrobial use (AMU) in animals, including aquatic animals, the environment and food. Since its designation in 2018, the UK’s FAO Reference Centre for AMR has engaged with more than 45 countries, providing expert advice and training to help tackle the AMR threat.

Since the conference, the AMR team at Cefas has hosted a delegation from the Department of Fisheries Malaysia and Universiti Putra Malaysia for training on the collection and analysis of environmental AMR samples, including an introduction to sequencing and bioinformatic analysis. We have also carried out three scoping visits to collaborators' laboratories: the Aquatic Animal Health Laboratory Services Centre in Brunei Darussalam, the Fish Quality Control Laboratory in Nairobi, Kenya, and the Aquaculture Research Institute of Zambia in Kafue, Zambia. These visits are part of the planning for hands-on training in antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods, which involves exposing bacteria to different antibiotics in the laboratory to see which treatments are likely to work. The training will enable the collaborators to produce quality data for their respective AMR surveillance in aquaculture and the environment; contributing to UK and global commitments to combatting antimicrobial resistance.

title: International Men’s Day 2026: The Future Begins with Opportunity

content.content: On the 19th November, we celebrate International Men’s Day, highlighting positive role models and raising awareness of men’s well-being. The theme for 2026 is “The Future Is Everyone”. It is a powerful call for inclusion, equality, and collaboration, reminding us that building a better future requires everyone to have a seat at the table.
Within the Civil Service, this theme resonates deeply with the mission of Going Forward into Employment (GFiE).

GFiE has helped over 5,000 individuals join the Civil Service through a network of accredited pathways . Many of those finding a renewed sense of purpose through these Pathways are men who have faced significant barriers to employment—including veterans, prison leavers, care-experienced individuals, and carers.
As we reflect on this year’s theme, we want to shine a light on the men who have transformed their lives through GFiE, and the managers who gave them that crucial opportunity.
More Than Just a Job
A secure role in the Civil Service provides far more than a steady income; it provides stability, independence, and a renewed sense of self-respect.

Take Mark, for example, a veteran who joined HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) through the Veterans pathway. After a 30-year career in the Royal Air Force, transitioning to civilian life presented its own unique challenges . The true impact of his new role wasn't just felt in his day-to-day work, but at home.

For others, the GFiE pathway represents a vital second chance. Only a quarter of prison leavers secure a job within a year of release, despite the fact that a chance at employment can be pivotal in preventing reoffending.
One GFiE candidate who joined the Civil Service after leaving prison shared how this opportunity provided personal redemption and a stable foundation for his family:
A Call to Recruiting Managers

For existing civil servants and recruiting departments, this is a call for action. When you use the GFiE pathways, you are directly delivering transformational social value while bringing highly motivated, resilient individuals into your teams.

We know that recruitment can sometimes feel complex, but GFiE pathways are designed to do things differently, we use simplified job descriptions, streamlined applications and interviews to help candidates flourish. We also work closely with partner organisations to source candidates and provide ongoing support to both the individuals and their line managers.
The feedback from managers who have embraced these pathways is overwhelmingly positive. As one Line Manger from Scottish Government shared regarding a team member:
Looking Forward
This International Men’s Day, let’s celebrate the resilience of the men who have stepped forward into public service, bringing new voices and vital life experiences into our departments.

If you are a recruiting manager looking to fill a vacancy, consider how you can open a door for someone who just needs a chance to show their capability. By choosing a GFiE pathway, you aren't just filling a skills gap—you are changing a life, uplifting a family, and building a Civil Service that truly represents the society it serves.
To find out how your department can recruit through our life-changing pathways, explore our Going Forward into Employment Pathways, or reach out to the GFiE team today.
