title: Helping farmers access more water: Water Management Grant guidance now available

content.content: In August, we announced a drought support package for farmers. Drought over the summer and into the autumn has highlighted the importance of reliable water supplies for agriculture. Investing in water storage can help businesses manage increasing weather variability and maintain production during dry periods.

As part of that package, we committed up to £15 million to round 3 of the Water Management grant. The grant will help farmers invest in on-farm irrigation reservoirs and water storage tanks. This will help use water more efficiently and become more resilient to drought.

In this post, we share what the grant will fund and details of an upcoming webinar. You can also see how two farms have used funding from previous rounds to improve irrigation water storage on their farms.

Providing finance to support water storage projects is just one strand of our work to help farmers tackle the impacts of drought. We also outline the steps we're taking to make it easier for farmers to build on-farm reservoirs and get the permissions they need to use the water they store.
Water Management grant round 3

We’ve now published the Water Management grant round 3 guidance on GOV.UK to help you prepare an application. The grant is for farmers and growers that want to improve farm water resilience by increasing sustainable on-farm water storage for irrigated crop production.
The application window will open on 30 November 2026 and will close 23 February at 11:59pm.

The application window is open for 12 weeks. This is a competitive grant scheme, and applications are not prioritised based on when they are submitted. Take the time you need to prepare your application before submitting it.
In this round of the grant, we're offering:
The grant will cover up to 40% of eligible project costs.

If your application is successful, you may receive a conditional grant funding agreement before you secure planning permission and any abstraction licence. You must have the required permissions in place before you receive a grant payment. Water Resources East (WRE) have produced a practical guide for farmers and planners on design, permissions and environmental integration.

If the grant is significantly oversubscribed, we may prioritise projects based on location, farming sector, collaboration and whether the relevant permissions are already in place. Collaborative projects that deliver benefits across multiple farm businesses may offer better value by improving water resilience at a local scale.
Join our webinar
Join our webinar to learn about round 3 of the Water Management grant. We’ll explain who can apply, what the grant will fund and run through the application process.
The webinar will take place Thursday 26 November at 11am - 12:30pm.
Register to attend
To get the most from the webinar, read the guidance beforehand and bring along any questions. During the live Q&A, you’ll have the chance to put them directly to the team.
Making on-farm reservoirs easier to build and use

Alongside the Water Management Grant, we are taking steps to make it easier for farmers to build and use on-farm reservoirs. We know that financing a new reservoir is one barrier, but getting planning approval and abstracting licensing are also concerns.
Defra and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) are developing a package of measures for on-farm reservoirs, supported by the Farming & Food Partnership Board (FFPB).

At the October board meeting, members helped us to identify the barriers farmers face when building reservoirs. They highlighted issues with financing, obtaining planning approvals and navigating abstraction licensing. Building on the Water Management Grant, we are exploring actions to help in all of these areas.
Making the planning process clearer

In August, we published our response to the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) consultation. It makes clear that local authorities should support the development of agricultural infrastructure, including reservoirs. The new NPPF confirms reforms to make planning policy easier to use. These reforms aim to support faster, simpler local plans and provide a clearer basis for planning decisions.

To give farmers more clarity and confidence when investing in water resilience, MHCLG will soon publish updated Planning Practice Guidance (PPG) for on-farm reservoirs. This has been developed in consultation with the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) and Country Land & Business Association (CLA).

We will continue to review evidence on how well current permitted development rights work for on-farm reservoirs. Defra and MHCLG are working with farmers and industry representatives, including the NFU and CLA, on this review. We hope to publish an update in due course.
We aim to make it easier for farmers to invest in water storage by improving planning guidance and making the process for getting the necessary permissions clearer.
Supporting long-term investment through abstraction licences

In the longer term, capturing water during wetter periods can reduce pressure on rivers during the growing season. This can help farm businesses become more resilient to drought while supporting sustainable food production. However, farmers and growers need confidence that they will be able to fill a reservoir before making the significant investment needed to build one. Abstraction licensing has an important role in supporting investment in new on-farm water storage.

Difficulty securing a long-duration abstraction licence can make it harder to finance long-term investment in sustainable abstraction practices. As part of the package announced on 1 October to help farmers access water, the Environment Agency has made it easier for farmers to apply for long-duration abstraction licences that better support this investment.

Looking ahead, the Environment Agency is continuing to explore how it can further support farmers to secure water and invest in long-term resilience, while ensuring abstraction remains sustainable and protects the environment.  This includes piloting new technology that uses real-time monitoring, telemetry and digital tools to help farmers dynamically abstract water, maximising opportunities to take water when it is available while protecting the environment when it is not.
Read the Environment Agency blog for full details of the abstraction changes and information on how to apply for a licence.
Case studies
FM Green & Son: securing water for crop growth
FM Green & Son is a family farming partnership run by Mark Green and his parents, Frank and Jean. The business has operated since 1960.

The farm grows potatoes and beetroot. It supplies potatoes for crisps in their own factory and also Walkers in Leicester. The beetroot is produced for pickling and bottling. Before securing grant funding, limited water availability meant the farm sometimes had to ration water, making it harder to irrigate crops consistently.
With support from a previous round of the Water Management Grant, the farm built 3 clay-lined reservoirs and connected them to its existing irrigation system.

The farm can now irrigate crops more consistently and has expanded production into parsnips and carrots. It has increased the area it can irrigate by 126 acres, in addition to the 550 acres it already irrigated. The farm can also supply water to a neighbouring farm, supporting collaboration, as well as productivity and business growth.
Allpress Farms: building resilience through water storage

Allpress Farms is a fourth-generation family farming business based at Holly House Farm near Chatteris. It is one of the UK’s largest leek growers. The business grows about 10,000 tonnes of leeks on around 400 hectares each year. It supplies major supermarkets, including Sainsbury’s, Waitrose, and Lidl. Through the local Greenshoots grower group, it also markets around 8,000 tonnes of red and brown onions each year.

The project focused on Hubbersteads Farm, a 222-hectare holding that Allpress Farms has rented for more than 40 years. The farm grows onions, leeks, beetroot, sugar beet and winter wheat. Its existing water supply could not meet irrigation needs, putting crop yield, quality and productivity at risk.
With support from the Water Management Grant, the business built a 36,444 cubic metre clay-lined winter-storage reservoir to support a summer abstraction licence of 22,700m3.

The project has increased water storage and improved resilience to drought and low rainfall. New irrigation and water management techniques help the business use water more efficiently. Better irrigation for onions, leeks, beetroot and sugar beet supports more consistent crop yield and quality and helps the farm produce food more sustainably as pressure on water supplies increases.
Keep up to date

Subscribe to the Farming blog to receive an update when round 3 of the Water Management grant opens. We’ll also let you know when we publish further guidance on planning permission and abstraction licences.

title: A day in the life of a Senior Pensions Consultant at GAD

content.content: After 15 years working in pensions, mainly in the public sector, I thought I had a fairly good idea of what to expect from the senior pensions consultant role at GAD. I was wrong! It has been far more interesting and varied than I could have possibly imagined.

I have worked on everything from pensions dashboards and scheme data to administration governance, procurement and performance measures, and supporting our fantastic team. No two days have been quite the same, but they have all had one thing in common: helping public service pension schemes turn complex challenges into practical ways forward.
So, a typical day? It is genuinely challenging to put this to paper. The variety is one of the things I enjoy most about the role.
Starting with the bigger picture
My day will often begin by taking stock of several different projects, each at a different stage and with its own priorities.

One piece of work might involve helping a client consider whether its pension administration performance measures are clear, proportionate and capable of encouraging the right behaviours. Another could focus on improving the quality of data used for an actuarial valuation. Alongside that, I might be preparing for a cross-government working group or discussing an emerging policy issue with colleagues.
Although these projects can look materially different, they are ultimately connected by the same objective: helping schemes deliver the right outcomes for their members.

Pensions administration is about much more than completing processes within a specified number of days. It is about ensuring that members receive the correct benefits, at the right time, supported by good data, effective controls and clear accountability which support an improved member experience.
A significant part of my role is helping clients step back from the detail and consider that wider picture and to enable them to connect the dots that they may have struggled to see in isolation.
Turning complexity into practical advice
One of the most interesting aspects of being a Senior Pensions Consultant is working at the intersection of policy, administration and real-life delivery.

A policy or contractual requirement may look unremarkable and straightforward on paper, but it also needs to work in practice. That means asking questions such as: Is the requirement measurable? Is the necessary data available? Who owns the process? What happens when something goes wrong? More pertinently, does it support the right outcome for the scheme and its members?

Recent work has included supporting the review of pension administration key performance indicators and service-level agreements. This involves looking through the numbers themselves and considering whether measures cover areas such as timeliness, accuracy, quality, member experience and operational resilience. It also means being alert to unintended consequences, because a poorly designed target can encourage teams to focus on what is easiest rather than member outcomes.
Clients need clear, proportionate and workable recommendations. Translating a complex pensions problem into something that supports a decision is one of the most rewarding parts of the job.
Working with people across different disciplines
By mid-morning, I may be in a client workshop, meeting with colleagues or reviewing work produced by a project team.

Collaboration is central to how we work. A single project might bring together pensions consultants, actuaries, analysts, data specialists, policy and business change professionals and client teams. Everyone brings a different perspective, and the strongest outcomes come from combining those perspectives rather than approaching a problem through one professional angle.

For example, when looking at valuation data, an actuarial colleague may focus on whether the information is suitable for calculations and experience analysis. My administration perspective adds questions about where the data originated, how it has been maintained, which operational processes affect it and what improvements could prevent the same issues recurring at the next valuation.

As a senior consultant, my role is often to bring those different strands together. That can mean creating the scope of a project, leading a workshop, challenging an assumption or making sure that the final advice remains grounded in the client’s practical constraints.
Looking ahead to new challenges
Pensions is an industry that never stands still, and part of my day is often spent looking ahead.

Pensions dashboards are a great example. The immediate focus for schemes may be connecting successfully and meeting the relevant requirements, but the longer-term questions are just as important. How will dashboards affect member expectations? What will they reveal about data quality? How should schemes monitor their service after connection? How can the information presented help members better understand their retirement provision and future pensions adequacy?

I support a cross-government working group where public service pension schemes can share their experiences, raise common challenges and learn from one another. The discussions can move quickly from detailed questions about particular benefit types to much broader issues of governance, data, testing and member engagement.
That combination of technical detail and strategic thinking is one of the things that makes the role so engaging.
Learning from experience and continuing to develop
Although I have worked in pensions for 15 years, joining GAD has given me opportunities to use that experience in new ways.

My background is mainly in public service pensions administration, so I understand many of the operational pressures that schemes and administrators face. At GAD, I can use that experience across a much broader range of projects, while learning from colleagues with expertise in actuarial work, policy, modelling, data and consultancy.

I have also had the opportunity to take on responsibilities beyond individual client projects. These have included supporting recruitment, guiding the wider team on specific areas, contributing to the development of our services and helping colleagues share their knowledge through industry blogs and events.

One of the biggest adjustments has been moving from roles where I was responsible for managing a particular service or scheme to a consultancy environment where the challenge is to understand a new problem quickly, ask the right questions and provide independent advice.
It has been a learning curve, but an extremely positive one.
Finishing the day with a different list

By the end of the day, I may have reviewed a data-audit specification, drafted client advice, discussed a project risk, prepared material for a workshop and helped resolve a technical pensions question.

I will usually finish with a slightly different to-do list from the one I started with. That is simply the nature of consultancy and pensions: priorities evolve, new questions emerge and conversations often open-up opportunities to explore an issue more deeply.
The work can be demanding, particularly when several complex projects are moving at the same time. However, it is also extremely rewarding.

Public service pensions affect millions of people. Behind every dataset, performance measure or project plan are members who need their pension to be calculated correctly, communicated clearly and paid when it is due.
Knowing that my work contributes to those outcomes gives the role a real sense of purpose.
A role with variety and impact
Just over a year into my time at GAD, what stands out most is the breadth and depth of the opportunity.

For anyone who enjoys solving problems, working with people and turning pensions expertise into practical improvements, it is a role with variety, challenge and the opportunity to make a genuine difference.
And while I still cannot describe a typical day, I am quite happy for it to stay that way.

title: New innovation funding to test technologies for water quality and soil health

content.content: Applications are now open for the Farming Innovation Programme (FIP) 'Healthy Soils and Water for a Sustainable Environment' competition.
Up to £28 million is available for projects that support innovation to improve soil health, water quality and environmental management in livestock and cropping systems on farms in England.
This competition supports practical innovation that helps farmers, growers and foresters manage these connected challenges in commercial settings.

The government’s ‘Farming Roadmap 2050: Growing England’s Future’ outlines the importance of healthy soils and clean water for resilient farm businesses and securing domestic food security. They support crop and grass growth, help farms make better use of nutrients and support a healthy natural environment.
In this post, we cover who can apply, what the competition will fund, key dates and case studies from previous innovation projects.
Overview of the fund
Delivered in partnership with Innovate UK, the competition is looking for projects that take a practical, joined-up approach to soil health, water quality and environmental management.
Farmers, growers or foresters must be involved throughout the project, so solutions are developed with on farm uses at the heart of the work.
Projects must benefit England’s agricultural, horticultural or forestry sectors by developing practical solutions that can:

The project must be led by a UK-registered business, include at least one other business or research organisation, and have total costs between £1 million and £5 million. Projects can last up to 36 months.
How to apply
Before applying, read the full competition guidance on the Innovation Funding Service. It includes the full eligibility, scope and funding rules.
To help you apply you can watch the Innovate UK briefing for potential applicants or download the slides.
The application window is now open, and closes on 28 January 2027 at 11am.
All projects must start by 1 August 2027.

If you want help finding a business partner for this competition, Innovate UK Business Connect’s Agrifood team can help. You can also connect with others interested in this competition by joining the Innovate UK Farming Innovation Programme LinkedIn group.
Case studies

In 2024, we opened a nutrient management competition and awarded more than £15 million to projects developing new ways to improve nutrient use on farm and reduce environmental impact. Below we share some case studies from this previous competition.
Transforming slurry
ElentecBioAg is developing technology to treat dairy cow slurry, turning it into fertiliser nutrients that farmers can use on their own farms or sell on.

Project partners Harper Adams University, Mastek Engineering, Merigan and Stoic Options, were awarded over £800,000. The aim is to reduce costs, aid compliance with water regulations and reduce the UK’s reliance on imported artificial fertiliser.
Check out this video the project produced to understand more about their work:
Improving nutrient retention in poultry litter
Led by Black Bull Biochar, with partners, Avara Foods, SRUC and the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, this project aims to increase nutrient retention in poultry litter.

With funding of £760,000, it is developing ChickenChar, a range of biochar products designed to retain nitrogen and phosphorus in poultry litter. This will reduce ammonia emissions and lock in more phosphates when it’s applied to land as a fertiliser.

The benefits are, improved poultry health and welfare, better working conditions for farm staff, and more effective nutrient management when farmers use poultry manure as an alternative to artificial fertiliser, which saves the farmer money.
Optimising nitrogen application with satellite imagery

Led by Messium alongside the UK Agri-Tech Centre, The Allerton Project and H L Hutchinson, this project was awarded £759,382 to develop a digital tool that uses satellite data and artificial intelligence (AI) to help farmers decide when and how much nitrogen fertiliser to apply. It combines information about conditions across the field with weather data to support these decisions.

The tool aims to help farmers, agronomists and growers make better use of nitrogen fertiliser, cut costs and reduce environmental impacts such as leaching, run-off and emissions which will be assessed during the project. Developed with feedback from farmers and other users, the tool is intended to be easy to use. In future, it could also support other crops and decisions about grazing.

The project is now in month 23 of 30, with two seasons of testing on working farms completed across the UK. According to the team trials are showing great promise for the developed platform, with Messium's nitrogen recommendations driving gross margin improvements of over £75/ha above Farm Standard in the best performing fields.
Environmental monitoring funding supports new competition

The new Healthy Soils and Water for a Sustainable Environment competition compliments the work of Defra, Innovate UK and the Natural Environment Research Council's (NERC) Innovation in Environmental Monitoring (IEM) programme. This programme aims to strengthen the UK’s environmental monitoring sector by developing and testing new sensing technologies. It awards funding for projects that can be commercialised, supporting both economic growth and closer collaboration between the public and private sectors.
Through our new competition applicants are able to incorporate water and soils monitoring of livestock and crop production systems in their bid, in order to tackle run off and leaching.

Verdant Carbon, alongside the National Institute of Agricultural Botany (NIAB) received funding from the IEM to explore a novel testing methodology for assessing soil biological health. The work looked at soil microbial communities and translated information on what they were doing for soil health into a simple metric that could be understood and used by landowners.

The funding helped test the approach by studying microbes in the soil and growing plants in large soil samples. Researchers measured plant growth to understand how well crops might grow and how healthy the soil was. This helped develop a soil health testing service for farmers.

title: Shaping the future of driving instructor training, together

content.content: We've been working closely with the driver training industry on changes that can strengthen the profession, improve the journey to becoming an approved driving instructor (ADI) and help learners receive consistently high-quality training.

No immediate action is needed on your part, but we want to keep you updated. This blog post covers changes to the car driver training and testing forum, our proposals to improve the ADI Part 2 test and what comes next for the ORDIT (Official Register of Driving Instructor Trainers) scheme.
Making the forum and workstreams more effective

At the May forum, we agreed to review the forum's structure and membership. We've since introduced clearer, more consistent membership criteria so the core forum remains focused, representative and manageable.

Going forward, the forum will concentrate on strategic discussion and agreeing shared goals and priorities for the industry. It will be supported by dedicated workstreams that take forward detailed work, reporting back to the forum.

The first Progress and Protect the Profession workstream meeting took place this month. It focussed particularly on the ADI Part 2 changes and the trainer and ORDIT discussions, building on work already carried out.

Forum membership is organised through recognised associations, which can help you stay informed, share your views and contribute to discussions that shape the profession. We also want to broaden the ways you can communicate with us directly, including more webinars and, in future, customer panels.
Improving the ADI Part 2 test
At the October forum, we presented proposals for ADI Part 2 developed from previous workshops with the industry, practitioner feedback and legal advice.

The aim is to strengthen the test within the current legislative framework so it better assesses the capabilities most relevant to professional driving instructors, helps Potential Driving Instructors (PDI) understand the skills, responsibilities and standards expected and improves their preparation for their ADI Part 3 test.
The proposed changes include:

Expert explanation and demonstration would operate across different parts of the assessment, with candidates explaining and demonstrating their knowledge, including how they manage risk, rather than giving short factual answers. This could include a stationary element and an on-road element, with questions varied across road types and conditions to reduce the risk of scripted answers.
There has been a lot of speculation and interest in these changes, so we wanted to share the plans with you early because of the scale of preparation involved.

We now need to start planning ADI examiner training, work with industry to develop supporting content such as the assessment and marking guide and allow our digital team time to plan the system changes needed to support the new test. Sharing our thinking early gives everyone, including trainers, PDIs and our own examiners, the best chance to prepare properly.
As part of this work, we will make sure the changes are accessible and that reasonable adjustments continue to support disabled candidates through the Part 2 test.

We are aiming to launch the changes to part 2 test in Spring 2027. Once everything is finalised, we'll make sure we give you a minimum of 3 months' notice before they take effect so you can prepare any changes to your business models, your approach to studying and training for qualification tests.

We will be talking more about the changes at our webinar on 25 November at 7pm. An invitation with the link to join the webinar was emailed to all ADIs and PDIs earlier in November. We will be sending a reminder invitation closer to the time.
We'll continue developing the detail with industry through the Progress and Protect the Profession workstream.
Next steps for ORDIT

In June, we brought industry partners together to look afresh at the ORDIT scheme. The workshop identified challenges with the current voluntary scheme, including low participation, inconsistent standards and limited assurance of trainer quality.
At this forum, we shared an early concept for a possible future approach. This is a starting point for discussion, not an agreed final scheme.
Discussion was broadly supportive of continuing to develop a scheme to replace ORDIT, but significant work remains before a final model can be agreed.

ADI representatives were clear that this needs to remain a priority and asked for a firm commitment to a replacement scheme, rather than leaving the position left by the previous ORDIT arrangements unresolved. We've heard that message. Separate legal advice is still awaited on the existing ORDIT scheme, and we'll communicate what happens next once that's received.

We'll continue gathering feedback from you, and use that evidence, alongside the forum discussion, to keep developing options for a replacement scheme. We will continue to work with the forum and workstream on this so that any future approach is credible, useful and supports better outcomes for everyone involved.
Keep working with us

These changes are about making industry engagement more useful and turning discussion into action. Workshops, workstreams, webinars and future customer panels will also all help us bring a wider range of experience into the work.

We'll continue to keep you updated on Part 2 changes and the future approach to ORDIT. In the meantime, make a note in your diary for the webinar on 25 November, and keep sharing your views through your association, your employer and the direct engagement opportunities we provide.
For more information about the issues discussed and the agreed next steps, read the full summary report from the October forum meeting.

title: UK NSC consults on screening for ovarian cancer

content.content: The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) is today opening a consultation on evidence relating to screening for ovarian cancer.

We are asking stakeholder organisations and individuals, including members of the public, to provide feedback on an evidence map and a draft recommendation that the UK NSC should archive its recommendation on ovarian cancer screening.
How to respond

To take part in the consultation, download the consultation documents by clicking on the grey ‘View documents’ button on the UK NSC’s ovarian cancer recommendation page. Then submit your response by clicking on the green ‘Submit comments’ button.
The deadline for responses is 11.59pm on 11 February 2027.
About ovarian cancer
Ovarian cancer occurs when abnormal cells grow uncontrollably in the ovaries, fallopian tubes or surrounding tissue, and can spread to other parts of the body.
Evidence base
The UK NSC does not currently recommend population screening for ovarian cancer.

This recommendation was informed by results from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS), which found that screening did not reduce deaths from ovarian cancer after 11 years of follow-up. At that time, the UK NSC agreed to reconsider the evidence when longer-term results from the trial became available.

Following publication of the longer-term UKCTOCS findings, the UK NSC commissioned an evidence map to assess whether the new evidence could affect its recommendation. Evidence maps help the UK NSC decide whether more in-depth evidence review work is needed.

The updated trial results, based on a median follow-up of 16.3 years, continued to show no statistically significant reduction in deaths from ovarian and tubal cancer with either screening strategy used. The evidence map therefore concluded that this new evidence was unlikely to change the UK NSC’s existing recommendation against population screening.

The evidence map also did not support commissioning a further evidence summary, and the recommended next step is to archive the recommendation. Archiving would mean that the UK NSC would not routinely review the topic of ovarian cancer screening again unless new evidence becomes available that is likely to significantly affect the existing recommendation.
Stakeholders can submit annual call proposals for the UK NSC to reopen any archived topics if new evidence becomes available.
Keep up to date

The UK NSC blog provides up to date news from the UK NSC. You can register to receive updates direct to your inbox, so there is no need to keep checking for new articles. If you have any questions about this blog article, or about the work of the UK NSC, please email uknsc@dhsc.gov.uk.

title: Inaccurate reporting on the Visitor Levy

content.content: On 4 November, we introduced the Visitor Levy Bill in Parliament, which is the next step towards giving local leaders powers to invest in their high streets, cultural sites, and tourist attractions and boost their local economies.
However, there has been media reporting suggesting that an overnight levy could add as much as £100 to a typical family break to London.

This figure is misleading. For this to be true, a family would need to spend around £2,000 on accommodation during their stay in London with a levy at 5%. And any estimated cost of a London levy is entirely hypothetical because London has not yet set out its exact plans for one.

For a typical family break, we estimate the cost to be much lower, with a 1% levy adding around £4 to the average three-to-four-night break for a family of four in England and a 5% levy adding around £20. This is based on VisitBritain data on holidays with children in England.
Reporting has also suggested that the levy could lead to 33,000 job losses. We don’t recognise this figure, and it is based on uncertain assumptions about the impact of a levy on visitor spending.

The levy is also designed so that decisions are taken locally, businesses must be consulted before a levy is introduced, and lower-cost stays will have proportionately low charges – protecting budget holidays and taking businesses’ views into account.
And visitor levies are already commonplace internationally, including in cities in Germany, Italy and the United States.
All the money raised will stay in the local area and can be reinvested to boost the visitor economy, including in transport, high streets, public spaces and events.

We can already see the benefits of the levy in Greater Manchester, with a £1 per room per night charge in 2023 raising £2.8 million in its first year. The revenue raised has supported the city’s success in hosting the first BRIT Awards to be staged outside of London, as well as the 2026 Women’s Cricket World Cup, showing how impactful even a small charge can be for visitors and the local economy.
Local leaders who choose to introduce a levy will be able to set out their plans for how the money raised would be invested from early 2028.

title: APHA's mapping experts are turning data into decisions

content.content: Many people associate geographic information systems (GIS) with maps. But in my work at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), I see that their real value is often in something much bigger: helping people turn complex data into information they can actually use.

One of my favourite examples is ibTB, our free online mapping service for sharing information about bovine tuberculosis (bTB). ibTB has been around since 2015 and was developed to make detailed information about bTB incidents available at the individual herd level, helping farmers and others in the livestock industry make more informed decisions about disease risk and biosecurity.

Over the last decade ibTB has continued to evolve. The recent introduction of bTB test history and movement information for individual animals  in England represents another major step forward in that journey. As we celebrate GIS Day, I thought it was a good opportunity to look at how ibTB has developed and some of the work that goes on behind the map.
Why location matters
Bovine TB remains one of the most significant animal health challenges facing Great Britain, with disease control costing taxpayers more than £150 million a year.

But disease data is not just about numbers. It is also about place. Every herd and every disease incident has a location. Putting this information on an interactive map can make disease patterns and local risks much easier to understand than they might be from rows of data or a report.

That thinking was fundamental to the development of ibTB, and in 2015 Defra committed to making detailed bTB information available at individual herd level so that farmers could make more informed, or “knowledge-based”, decisions about bTB biosecurity.

Today, having this kind of information available online may not seem particularly unusual. But making disease information available geographically and at individual herd level gives farmers a new way of understanding the disease situation around them.
Helping farmers make informed choices

One of the important ideas behind ibTB is something called risk-based trading. Put simply, when farmers buy cattle, disease risk can be considered alongside the other information they use to make purchasing decisions.

ibTB allows the farming community to explore current bTB incidents as well as incidents that have closed during the previous ten years. This gives users a way of exploring both an individual herd's history and the wider disease picture in the surrounding area.

The introduction of the Health Rating added another useful piece of information. It shows the number of years a herd has been clear of bTB, providing a simple measure designed to encourage informed trading.

This is ultimately about giving users good quality information that allows them to make informed decisions. And farmers have certainly made use of the service. Since its launch, the site has been visited more than 1.5 million times and receives around 1,200 unique users each month, meaning 1,200 individual people visit the site, regardless of how many times each person visits.
From herds to individual animals

Perhaps the most exciting recent development has been the move beyond information about herds to information about individual animals in England. Interestingly, this is not a completely new ambition. When future developments for ibTB were being considered some years ago, adding individual animal data was already on the list of potential enhancements.

That ambition has now become a reality. For people using the system, the result is straightforward: more detailed information is available to help them understand disease risk related to the potential purchase of individual animals. Behind the scenes, however, it is a much bigger change.

Moving from information about herds to information about individual animals increases both the amount and the complexity of data that needs to be processed and prepared for publication. And this is where the part of GIS that users do not normally see becomes particularly important.
What happens behind the map?
When people use ibTB, they see a map. What they do not see is all the work taking place behind it.

My colleagues in APHA's Data Systems Group (DSG) and GIS teams work with data from operational and surveillance systems, preparing and checking it so that it can ultimately be presented through ibTB. As the amount and complexity of information grows, reliable data processing and quality assurance become increasingly important.

For me, that is one of the interesting things about modern GIS. The map may be the part everyone sees, but it is only the final stage in a much longer journey. Before information reaches that map, data has to be brought together, processed, checked and transformed into something that can be used by the service.

The addition of individual animal information has made that work even more important. It means dealing with larger and more complex datasets while still providing information in a way that is useful to the people accessing ibTB.
It is a good reminder that successful GIS is not only about making good maps. It depends just as much on accurate data, reliable processes and the people behind them.
What the ibTB journey shows us

ibTB today looks very different from the service that launched in 2015. It started by making herd-level bTB information available through an online GIS. Since then, developments such as Health Ratings have added new ways for users to understand disease history, while the introduction of individual animal information in England has taken the level of detail available another significant step forward.
There will always be opportunities to improve how we use data and technology to communicate animal health information. But I think the journey so far already demonstrates something important.

GIS is often described as a way of putting data onto a map. In reality, it can do much more than that. It can bring together complex information and make it more understandable and useful to the people who need it.

ibTB is a great example. What began as a way of publishing herd-level disease information has continued to evolve as technology, data and the needs of users have changed. For me, that is what makes it a particularly good story for GIS Day.

Behind what appears to be a relatively simple map is animal health science, data, technology and a lot of work by people across APHA and beyond, all coming together to help livestock keepers make better-informed decisions.

title: Professional curiosity: looking beyond the obvious

content.content: Professional Curiosity: looking beyond the obvious - Blog by Tamara Cooper

One day, many years ago, I visited a house it the UK. I worked for the police and neighbours had reported the sounds of a disturbance. When I arrived, a female opened the door and invited me in. The female was home alone. It was a very nice house, immaculate in fact and the female took me into the large kitchen where I explained the purpose of my visit. We talked for some time, and the female denied any disturbance and said that everything was fine. I just felt something was not quite right. She appeared nervous and was constantly taking a hair band on and off her hair. I tried different ways to engage with the female, but she was unable to talk about her life. I felt an over-whelming sense of hopelessness in this beautiful home, but could I not reach her.
As I got up to leave, I saw a dog bowl in the corner of the kitchen. I said to the female, how lovely, where is your dog?
There was no dog.
The bowl was where the female was forced by her partner to eat her meals.

You may consider this to have been a demonstration of professional curiosity. In truth, I was desperately looking for a way in, a way to reach someone I instinctively felt to be frightened and at risk.

All practitioners from all agencies are likely to be familiar with the term professional curiosity. We are quite adept at using language skilfully and creatively, but what do we actually mean by advocating the use of professional curiosity?

In my view, this is about being wholly emotionally and intellectually present and being willing to look beyond what appears obvious. People who have seldom been heard or are actively being abused or neglected are unlikely to find it easy to communicate their truth and it is possible that they are the very people who will be targeted by those who seek to hurt other people because of their vulnerabilities and the perception that they are less likely to be believed or validated.
Despite the indefatigable efforts of many professionals, there remain some who proceed to judge and minimalise the lived experience of people using services.
Consider these two scenarios.

Scenario 1; Beryl is eighty-eight and lives in a care home. Beryl reports to her daughter that she has been sexually assaulted by a carer. The manager of the care home tells police that Beryl has a UTI and does get confused and exhibits early signs of dementia. The police leave and record no crime. They do not speak to Beryl. They do not know if Beryl has capacity. They do not see Beryl. They do not hear Beryl. Beryl is invisible. The offender is free to abuse someone else.

Scenario 2; As scenario 1 but police do not rely on the word of the manager. They visit Beryl. Beryl does have capacity. Beryl can give an account of her assault. Beryl is heard. Beryl is not invisible. Beryl is safe. The offender is arrested and charged. Vulnerable victims are safeguarded.

In my current role in policing, with a national, regional and local focus on adults at risk, I am often heard to say to my colleagues and partners, you must turn up, suspend judgment and genuinely open your eyes and ears and ask the questions that may get an answer. People who need our help and those who love them are seeking assurance right now that we will turn up for them and people who want to harm may try to disrupt us in doing so. Do not be a passive bystander if your instinct is telling you something isn’t right, it probably isn’t.

Experience over years has led me to believe that it can be just one person who shines a light in a dark tunnel that enables someone previously unable to communicate their truth. One social worker, one teacher, one police officer, one human who stops by long enough to see and hear the journey towards this day. Be determined to be that person. You may change a life or safeguard someone in a way that they did not think was possible.

title: Black Tech Fest: learning for an inclusive digital government
authors: Thomas Beautyman, Deputy Director Digital Capability and Workforce

content.content: Black Tech Fest brought together conversations about inclusive artificial intelligence (AI), cyber resilience and routes into government technology careers. On 29 October 2026, we attended Black Tech Fest at Tobacco Dock in London.
The festival connects technologists, creatives and innovators. Organisers advertised this year’s event for 5,000 attendees, with more than 100 speakers.
Government participants included:
Kalbir’s and Bella’s sessions connected the day’s conversations with our work to develop digital and cyber skills.
Listening to people interested in government technology

At the joint Government Digital and Data Profession and Government Cyber Profession stand, hundreds of people stopped to talk. Many wanted to understand what government does in technology and how they could get into cyber. Their questions included:
These conversations gave us a chance to explain government’s technology work and help people understand how they could contribute.

To transform public services, government needs to attract, retain and develop people with digital skills. Black Tech Fest was an opportunity to reach people from diverse backgrounds who may not have considered government technology careers. Listening to their questions is part of making those careers more accessible.
Broadening participation and building trust in AI

In 'Is the UK Ready for AI?', Kalbir connected participation in the AI economy with access to government services. He highlighted two priorities: enabling a wide range of people to contribute to technological change, and making sure everyone can get the core services they need.
Building trust in AI starts with being open about how it is used. Kalbir set out the questions people need answered about AI in a service:
He pointed to algorithmic transparency records as a practical way of making that use more visible.

This sits alongside our wider work to accelerate the responsible adoption of AI across the public sector. We’re working with departments to identify opportunities, strengthen technical capability and ensure AI is deployed safely, ethically and at scale.
Taken together, the connection for our work was clear: inclusion means both who shapes technology and who benefits from it.
Preparing for evolving cyber threats
Bella joined the panel 'Are We Ready for the Next Generation of Cyber Threats?'. A key lesson was the need to consider risks across government, not just within individual organisations.

The discussion explored investment to improve understanding of the technology used across government, helping teams respond to and recover from cyber threats. It also covered work under the Government Cyber Action Plan to support this effort.
Another focus was using innovation to strengthen cyber defence, including adopting frontier AI.

Collaboration was another theme: organisations do not face these complex security challenges alone. Security leaders have a role in bringing people together across organisational boundaries to explore innovation and manage risk.
Together, the sessions highlighted the need for services that are understandable and dependable, backed by people with the skills to build and secure them.
Finding your route into government technology
There are several routes into government technology, whether you are exploring an apprenticeship, looking for a role that fits your skills or returning after a career break.
Apprenticeships through TechTrack

TechTrack combines structured learning with practical experience in government digital and cyber roles. About 100 TechTrack apprentices now work across government, bringing experience from a range of backgrounds and career paths.
Other digital, data and cyber career routes
Beyond apprenticeships, explore the following to see where your skills and interests could fit:
Returning to technology after a career break
The Returnship Programme is for people who have been out of work for 18 months or more. It offers 18 months of experience before participants can apply for a full-time role within their teams.

Developed with the Ministry of Justice and Home Office, the pilot focused on senior software developer roles. The programme aims to diversify the profession and bring experienced people back into technology.
Preparing an application
The Government Digital and Data Candidate Information Pack offers further guidance on these pathways and tips for applying.
Developing skills in public service

Developing skills also means supporting people already working in public service. Civil servants and UK public sector colleagues can access free learning and certification pathways through Get Tech Certified until 31 December 2026.
The Women in Tech learning offer brings together learning, events and opportunities to connect, supporting women across the public sector to develop their skills and careers.
Taking the learning forward

Black Tech Fest helped us connect government’s technology work with people interested in contributing. This outreach sits alongside TechTrack and the Returnship Programme as part of a wider effort to broaden participation and develop the people who build and secure public services.

title: One year of the Company Data Layer
authors: Pedro Pinto Da Silva, Senior Data Architect

content.content: The complexity surrounding business support

Business support is at the core of the government’s economic growth mission. To meet the diverse needs of businesses and remove barriers to growth, the government relies on a wide range of digital services. This digital support offer is complex and to be effective, it must be well connected and coherent.
Business needs can be described through research, but data is also needed to deliver value to them through a complex network of services.

Company data tells us who businesses are such as their size, location and financial performance. Advisers use business profiles to identify businesses most likely to benefit from government support. Digital systems use profile data to create personalised workflows and reduce the data entry burden.
Until recently, however, the value of company data was offset by the work required to use it.
Across BIST, teams and individuals:
Introducing the Company Data Layer
A year ago, we set out to change this. We wanted to create one reusable source of company data that could allow teams from across BIST to access what they need.

We created the Company Data Layer (CDL), a common component for company data that does the work once. It gives services a simple way to find reliable company information, without each team sourcing, cleaning and maintaining its own data. Over the last year, the CDL has demonstrated its value in real services. We have reliably delivered insights to our internal CRM, the application and case management systems for the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme (BICS), and other services across BIST.
After 6 months of being in beta, we can reflect on the CDL’s impact on our services and look ahead to future possibilities.
How BIST is benefiting from the Company Data Layer
Improving data quality across the support ecosystem

When services can identify businesses reliably, the data they collect becomes more useful and easier to reuse. Easy access to business identification tools, like search and data matching, helps teams capture recognised identifiers earlier in the user journey. This improves downstream data linking and use.
Speeding up digital product and service delivery

Using or searching through company data is now as easy as making an Application Programming Interface (API) request or consuming an integration event. Teams can remove the burden of sourcing, cleaning and storing company data and focus on creating the compelling user experiences that make their products uniquely valuable. Michal Charemza, Lead Data Engineer working on the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, says:
Martin Tierney is a Senior Software Engineer working on the Data Hub Customer Relationship Management (CRM) tool. He says:
Revealing data problems and complexity

Having a single source of data can simplify complexity and reveal and resolve discrepancies. Company data can be spread across sources and described in different ways, so simplifying and checking it required great manual effort before the CDL.
Smoother and more effective back-office processes

Improvements to data quality means it is easier to join the dots across the ecosystem to understand users and their activity. Cross-service activity provides invaluable contextual information to BIST advisers who need it to deliver effective support to businesses.
How the Company Data Layer has acheived this
While the Company Data Layer’s value is generated from widespread adoption, its success stems largely from its design features.
Users choose the CDL over alternatives because of extensibility, flexibility and resilience.
The CDL can be extended
We designed it to easily extend to more data sources as we acquire them by:
Flexibility is built in
We recognise that different services and users need to consume our data in different ways. The service supports:

Soon, we will support a connector for our internal AI tools, and a way of searching for lists of businesses based on customisable criteria. This will allow users to interact with the CDL using queries in English through their AI chat of choice. The combination of these features opens new opportunities, such as allowing our business advisors to find promising leads.

As we expand to more services, we help them access rich and consistent data allowing them to be smarter and more personal for their users. For example, the ability to look at a business’s history is critical for funding and grants leading to better decisions and reducing bureaucratic effort for businesses.
The CDL is designed for resilience

We have invested in the CDL’s resilience due to its importance for our infrastructure. It scales automatically based on demand. We now have a complete suite of alerts notifying the team of various problems, including slow responses, old data, or unusual traffic.

We work with the services using the CDL to ensure we have robust fallback mechanisms. This means that they can continue to operate if the CDL experiences any short-term issues. We now have the confidence to expand adoption at pace and onboard citizen-facing services.
What is next for the Company Data Layer?

Company data is used across government to support businesses and growth. If you work in local government or partner organisations such as the Growth Hub network and Chambers of Commerce, you likely face many of the same data challenges we faced in BIST.

Our ambition is to make the Company Data Layer accessible beyond BIST, so that other departments and organisations can benefit from it. We have built a service that is extendible, flexible and scalable from the ground up.

If you work with businesses, you can help us by sharing your interest in the CDL. Tell us who you are and what challenges you face with company data. We would be excited to showcase our service capabilities and supported use cases. Please get in touch at datamatching@businessandtrade.gov.uk.

title: Ten years of transparency: How Food Hygiene Ratings changed the way we choose where to eat
authors: Kathryn Baker, Chief Environmental Health Officer

content.content: As Northern Ireland marks ten years of mandatory Food Hygiene Rating display, we spoke to Kathryn Baker, Chief Environmental Health Officer at the Department of Health in Northern Ireland, about the development of the scheme, the importance of transparency and the people who have helped make it a success.

When choosing somewhere to eat, many of us look for the familiar green and black Food Hygiene Rating sticker displayed at food businesses. But ten years ago, displaying that rating wasn’t a legal requirement in Northern Ireland.
Today, the sticker is an established part of the food landscape, giving customers information about the hygiene standards found when a business was inspected.

For Kathryn Baker, who previously worked at the Food Standards Agency (FSA), leading on the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme in Northern Ireland, the tenth anniversary is a particularly meaningful milestone.

“The food hygiene rating scheme is very close to my heart, because before I joined the Department of Health, I worked in the Food Standards Agency and for many years I led on the development of the scheme in Northern Ireland.”
A decade of progress
The Food Hygiene Rating Scheme was introduced in Northern Ireland in 2010, with the FSA working alongside district councils to provide consumers with clear information about food hygiene standards.
The principle was straightforward: businesses would receive a rating from 0 to 5, giving consumers an easy way to understand the hygiene standards of a business.
However, while businesses were awarded ratings and consumers could check them online, displaying the rating at the premises was initially voluntary.
By 2013, evidence of the scheme’s impact was beginning to emerge, with 54% of businesses achieving the highest rating of 5.

In the years that followed, the proportion of businesses achieving the top rating continued to increase. By 2016, 70% of businesses were achieving a rating of 5, with the figure rising to 84% by 2026.
For Kathryn, that progress is an achievement worth recognising.
“That is a remarkable increase — and an achievement that belongs first and foremost to the food businesses and their staff who have worked hard to raise and maintain standards.”
But a significant change in 2016 helped make those standards more visible to consumers.
Ten years of transparency
On 7 October 2016, the Food Hygiene Rating Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 came into operation, making it a legal requirement for rated food businesses to display their Food Hygiene Rating.
Kathryn explained how this marked an important turning point in making food hygiene information more accessible.
“Before mandatory display, businesses were given ratings and consumers could access that information. But mandatory display put that information directly in front of the customer.”
“You didn’t need to search a website. You didn’t need to know that a rating existed. You simply walked through the door and it was there.”
The change meant that customers could see a business’s rating before deciding whether to eat there, while businesses had a visible way to demonstrate their hygiene standards.

A Food Hygiene Rating tells customers about the hygiene standards found at the time a business was inspected. Environmental Health Officers assess how food is handled, the cleanliness and condition of the premises, and how food safety is managed.

Businesses receive a rating from 0 to 5, with 5 indicating very good hygiene standards. The rating is not a review of the taste or quality of the food or the service provided. Instead, it gives people information to help them make informed choices about where they eat or order food.
Kathryn believes making this information visible has been one of the scheme’s most important achievements.
“That approach has helped create a culture where good food hygiene is not something that happens behind the scenes.”
“It is something businesses can demonstrate publicly. And consumers can see.”
A scheme recognised across Northern Ireland
Ten years on, the familiar green and black sticker has become widely recognised.
According to the FSA’s Food and You 2 research, 93% of people in Northern Ireland had heard of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme, while 95% recognised the rating sticker when shown it.
Research also found that 49% of people in Northern Ireland who eat out had checked a food business’s hygiene rating in the previous 12 months.
For Kathryn, these findings demonstrate the importance of making food hygiene information available to everyone.
“The rating is therefore doing exactly what it was intended to do: giving people information that helps them make informed choices.”
The scheme has become part of everyday life, helping consumers consider hygiene standards when deciding where to eat.
A partnership that works
While mandatory display has played an important role in the scheme’s development, Kathryn is clear that legislation alone cannot explain its success.
“But the food hygiene rating scheme cannot succeed through legislation alone. The real success story is the partnership and the people behind it.”
Northern Ireland’s eleven district councils and their Environmental Health Officers are at the heart of the scheme.
They carry out inspections, assess hygiene standards and work directly with businesses, while the FSA provides the framework and works with councils to ensure consistency.
Kathryn is keen to recognise the commitment of those involved.

“Our district councils and their environmental health professionals are at the heart of the system and I want to pay tribute to the Environmental Health Officers and food safety teams across Northern Ireland’s councils.”
“They inspect food businesses, assess compliance, provide advice and take enforcement action where necessary. Their role is vital and ultimately, it’s about protecting the public.”
Kathryn also recognises the work that takes place every day within food businesses to maintain good hygiene standards.

“Behind every rating is a team of people cleaning premises, controlling temperatures, preventing cross-contamination, managing food safety, training staff and putting effective food safety procedures into practice.”
“A rating of 5 doesn’t happen by accident. It reflects a sustained commitment to doing things properly.”
For Kathryn, the progress made over the past decade belongs to everyone who has contributed to making food hygiene standards more visible and helping consumers make informed choices.
Looking ahead to the next ten years
As the way people buy and order food continues to evolve, making food hygiene information accessible remains just as important.
Customers are increasingly making decisions online, whether booking a restaurant, ordering a takeaway or choosing somewhere new to eat.
Kathryn recognises a challenge for the years ahead is ensuring people continue to have access to the information they need, wherever they choose to buy food.
“Over the next ten years, our task is to make sure that same confidence follows consumers wherever they choose to buy their food, whether that be in person or online.”
And while the scheme has developed considerably since its introduction, its underlying purpose remains unchanged.
“When people have information, they can make informed choices and when businesses know that high standards are visible, there is a powerful incentive to maintain them.”

For Kathryn, ten years of mandatory Food Hygiene Rating display is about more than the familiar green and black sticker. It represents a decade of greater transparency, partnership and commitment to food hygiene standards across Northern Ireland.
“Because food safety is not simply about meeting a standard. It’s about earning the public’s trust.”
Check before you choose
Whether you’re visiting a restaurant, café or takeaway, look for the green and black Food Hygiene Rating sticker or check the business’s rating online at food.gov.uk/ratings.
Remember, a Food Hygiene Rating tells you about the hygiene standards found at the time of inspection, helping you make an informed choice.

title: Data-driven development management: consulting on England's first mandatory application data standard

content.content: Every year, England's local planning authorities (LPAs) receive more than 500,000 planning applications. This data has enormous potential to speed up decision-making, improve efficiency and give government, councils and communities a clearer picture of what is being proposed and where. But right now, there is no consistent, trusted foundation of planning application data, and no reliable way to find, analyse and build digital services around it.

This is largely because applicants often enter information in different formats when they complete an application form online. Some details a local planning authority (LPA) needs can be incomplete, or hard to find or understand. Planning officers have to follow this up, which adds time to the planning application process. Each council also stores this information differently, using different software that can make it hard for stakeholders to find, compare and use this data.

Consistent data at the point of application would enable the smooth flow through to later stages and make the whole process more efficient. It would also give developers of digital tools, including artificial intelligence (AI), a reliable foundation to build services that help LPAs, applicants and communities.

A data standard sets out exactly what information must be shared and how it should be structured. It means applicants know what to provide, and LPAs can accept, process and publish it more easily. That is why today we have launched a consultation on introducing the first mandatory planning application data standard in England.
What are we proposing

Using the planning data powers in the Levelling Up and Regeneration Act, we’re proposing regulations that will require all planning applications to be submitted and shared as consistent, structured, machine-readable data. The planning application standard will define the structure of information recorded at 2 key moments: when an application is submitted, and when a decision is reached. This will support a consistent, end-to-end data record of the planning permission process in England.

The initial planning application data standard will cover the data on the current planning application forms for the most common application types. It will also cover the data that must be published as open data from the application and decision process. Services that applicants use to submit applications will have to provide data in line with the standard. LPAs will then have to process and publish the data to the same specification.
Built collaboratively

One of the most significant aspects of this work is how we have done it. Since October 2024, we've designed the proposed planning application data standard collaboratively and in the open working with a community across government, local authorities, technology companies and established planning software providers. Members have contributed to, tested and challenged the emerging specification throughout its development. They have done this through community sessions and online forums, including GitHub (a web-based platform which facilitates collaborative development of software projects) and design.planning.gov.uk. This has been invaluable in verifying our approach and making sure the standard meets the needs of the people who use the planning system.

We have funded 5 pilot projects, through the Development Management Software Fund. These pilots have been working with each of the main back-office planning system providers used by LPAs across England to process planning applications, to test the standard in practice, help shape it and identify where more guidance is needed.

As a practical demonstration, we have developed a prototype form generator. This shows how planning application forms can be produced directly from the published data standard, demonstrating how the specification works in practice.

This collaborative, open approach is a template for how we will continue to unlock more planning data in the future. The tools and methods we have developed are repeatable, and we intend to use them as we expand the standard over time.
What this data standard means in practice

The open data published under the standard by LPAs will be compiled into a national data set on the Planning Data platform, making it easy to find, download and use. This includes access via an API (a way for other computer systems to automatically retrieve and use the data), allowing software developers, researchers and analysts to build tools and services directly from up-to-date planning data.
Once implemented the standard will:
Overall, a consistent approach across the country will make submitting a planning application a more predictable and transparent process, with the potential for faster validation and processing.
Have your say

The planning application data standard represents the start of a genuine step-change in how the planning system works and we want to hear from everyone affected by these proposals. The consultation document sets out the proposals including the scope of the initial standard, the approach to secondary legislation and the implementation timeframe.

We are particularly keen to hear from LPAs, software suppliers, developers and applicants, to make sure those most affected can help shape how the standard is implemented and works in practice. The consultation closes on 30 December 2026. We will then consider all responses as we finalise the regulations and our approach to implementation.
With the right data standard in place, we can get the planning system flowing more quickly, adopt new digital tools and services and make planning data available for everyone to see and use.
For more information
Have your say in the consultation on a planning application data standard.

Find out more about this work and register to take part on the data standards community homepage, where you'll also find updates and relevant links. The next meeting is on 25 November 2026 at 10:30am.

title: AI and coursework: how we can tackle this together

content.content: Coursework season is starting. If a student uses AI to do their coursework, they risk losing the whole qualification. And even if they're never caught, they lose the skills and understanding the coursework was meant to build. We're asking teachers for one honest conversation with their students about both, and we've built a toolkit that makes it easy.
What we're asking of teachers
Have one conversation with your students about the risks of using AI to do their coursework. The lesson plan, poster and assembly presentation are ready to use with no preparation.
The conversation in two points
The risk students know about

Using AI to do coursework and handing it in as your own is cheating. If it's discovered, a student can lose the whole qualification, not just the coursework mark. Last year, more than 1,100 students lost an entire GCSE or A Level.
The risk that's easier to miss

Even if a student is never caught, coursework exists to build skills and understanding they'll need later. If AI does the work, they don't build them. The grade may look fine, but it won't reflect what they can do, and the gap shows up when it matters.

You don't need to identify AI-generated work or decide where lines fall on specific uses. You need to make the case honestly, and most teachers already feel able to. In our September 2026 survey with Teacher Tapp, 85% of secondary teachers said they felt confident having a direct conversation with a student about AI use.
Why we think this will work
Students are most likely to listen to a trusted adult in their school, not a regulator. That's you.

A large study of students in a school system overseas found that heavier use of AI for schoolwork was linked to weaker exam results over time, even though it improved the homework students handed in. It's one study from a different system, so we wouldn't read its figures across to England. But it matches what teachers tell us.
If a student pushes back
You will probably hear some of these. You don't need a perfect answer. A calm, honest one is enough.
If a student says they're stuck, or has already used AI

Tell them to come to you. That is what we are telling them to do as well, so they will hear the same advice from us. A student who is stuck should ask their teacher. It is a much easier conversation to have then, than a malpractice investigation afterwards.
What's in the toolkit
Available now on Ofqual's Teacher Hub:
The bottom line

A student who hands in work AI produced isn't getting away with something. If they're caught, they can lose the qualification. If they're not, they've still lost the chance to build a skill they'll need. A short conversation now could help them see that before it matters.
We'd ask every school and college with coursework subjects to use the toolkit.
Jo Handford, Director of Assessment Integrity and Innovation, Ofqual

title: Best AI tools for coursework? There isn't one, and here's why that's worth knowing before you start

content.content: If you've searched for the best AI tool for helping you write your coursework – ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, or a writing aid like Grammarly or QuillBot – the clear answer is that there isn't a 'best' one. But that’s because using any of them to produce any part of your coursework is cheating.
If AI-produced work is submitted as your own, it can be identified and the consequences can include losing marks for the coursework or the entire qualification.
That's not the answer most 'best AI tools' roundups give you.
Why this isn't about which tool you use
The question that matters isn't which AI tool is best. It's not even really about AI tools at all. It's about whether the work you submit is actually yours.

The work has to be your own: your thinking, your research, your structure and your writing. And any AI use has to be declared, as your exam board's rules require. Declaring that AI wrote your answer doesn't turn it into your work, and work that is mostly your own can still get you into trouble if you hid that AI was involved.

Passing off work that AI produced as your own is the problem, and it can cost you the whole qualification. Exam boards and teachers are increasingly experienced at identifying work that isn't a student's own, including AI-generated content. The safest approach is simple: make sure the work you submit is genuinely yours and follow the rules on declaring any permitted AI use.
The risk you already know about

When AI-generated work is identified in coursework, the consequences can be severe. You can lose marks for the assessment, lose the qualification, and in the most serious cases face additional sanctions. These aren't theoretical risks. Cases are investigated every year, and students found to have cheated face significant consequences.
The risk that's easier to miss

There's another reason coursework should be your own. Coursework is designed to show what you know and can do. If AI produces the work, your submission no longer reflects your own knowledge, understanding and skills. That is exactly why submitting AI-generated work as your own is treated as malpractice.
A word of caution if you ever do ask AI something

If you ask an AI tool a question and it gives you facts, sources or quotes, don't take them on trust. Large language models are known to confidently state things that sound plausible but aren't true, including inventing sources that don't exist. That's one more reason the thinking in your coursework needs to be yours: you're the one who can tell when something's actually right.
If you're stuck, or you've already used AI
If you're turning to AI because you're stuck or not sure how to approach something, talk to your teacher instead. They are there to help, and it won't put your grade at risk.

If you've already used AI for your coursework, speak to your teacher now. It's far better to address the issue before submission than to face a malpractice investigation once the work has been reviewed.
The bottom line

There's no AI tool that's safe to use to produce your coursework, whatever its marketing says about being a study aid or a writing assistant. The question isn't which one is best. The question is whether it's worth risking your coursework marks, your qualification and a malpractice investigation. No AI tool can make that risk disappear.
Jo Handford, Director of Assessment Integrity and Innovation, Ofqual
