title: What could be hiding in imported raw meat for pet food: detecting antimicrobial resistance at the UK border

content.content: Some bacterial infections can be treated with antimicrobial drugs. But what if the bacteria responsible could no longer be treated effectively with antibiotics? Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is making that possibility increasingly real, allowing resistant bacteria to move silently through animals, food and the environment before reaching people. In reality, these bacteria can also cross national borders, meaning that what begins on a farm or in a food production setting has the potential to affect us all.

For World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week, we wanted to share a new project funded through the Integrated Security Fund and delivered with colleagues at Veterinary Medicines Directorate (VMD). It is exploring whether imported raw meat intended for pet food could provide a route for resistant bacteria and their genes to enter the United Kingdom (UK).

The project is called Antimicrobial Resistance Biosecurity at the Borders, or AMRBioBorders. It brings together border sampling, laboratory science, data analysis and policy expertise across government, to examine an area not currently covered by routine AMR surveillance.
Why antimicrobial resistance matters

Antibiotics are medicines used to treat bacterial infections, but bacteria can change over time and become resistant to the medicines used to tackle the infections they cause, making those infections harder to treat. Resistant bacteria can spread between people, animals and the environment, which is why tackling AMR requires a One Health approach that considers all three together. The UK has made good progress in reducing antibiotic use and resistance in food-producing animals, but bacteria do not respect borders. The movement of people, animals and products means we also need to monitor emerging threats from overseas.
Why look at raw pet food?

Raw pet food contains uncooked animal products such as meat and offal. Unlike cooked or heat-treated products, it does not undergo a step designed to kill bacteria before it is sold. This does not mean that every raw pet food product contains harmful or resistant bacteria. It does mean that careful production, storage and handling are important.

A recent Food Standards Agency survey examined 380 raw dog and cat food samples bought from shops and online retailers in the UK. Pathogenic bacteria were detected in 35% of the samples, and some of the bacteria found were also resistant to selected antibiotics. The Food Standards Agency advises owners to store, defrost and handle raw pet food safely to reduce the risk of cross-contamination.

Our project asks a different question: what can we learn by looking further upstream, at imported raw meat ingredients, intended to become raw pet food? At present, there is no routine AMR surveillance of imported raw meat at the UK border. We therefore may have an important gap in our understanding of what bacteria and resistance genes may be arriving through this route. Through AMRBioBorders, personnel at selected ports are collecting samples of imported raw meat ingredients destined for raw pet food and scientists at APHA are developing and applying computer-based methods to identify the bacteria and antimicrobial resistance genes within them.
Reading all the genetic clues at once

Traditionally, scientists investigate bacteria by growing them in the laboratory. This remains essential, but it can mean selecting particular organisms in advance. AMRBioBorders utilises a technique called metagenomic sequencing to look more widely.

Put simply, metagenomics allows us to examine genetic material from many different microorganisms, including bacteria, in a sample at the same time. Rather than asking only, “Is this particular bacterium present?”, we can look more widely at the microbial community and search for genes associated with AMR or disease.

Metagenomic findings would then help us select bacteria for traditional laboratory culture and whole genome sequencing. Comparing the results would allow us to assess how reliably the broader metagenomic approach detects organisms and resistance markers in this type of sample.
From scientific data to practical action

Generating data is only useful if people can act on it. This project, therefore, goes beyond the laboratory. It brings together APHA, Veterinary Medicines Directorate, Food Standards Agency, UK Health Security Agency, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, port authorities and others with responsibilities across the raw meat and pet food chain.

By mapping those responsibilities alongside the scientific evidence, the project could identify gaps, support more joined-up surveillance and help government decide where future monitoring would have the greatest value.

The findings could also help us work constructively with industry to build a better evidence base, identify where risks may be mitigated and support proportionate decisions that protect animal and public health.
Building a clearer picture

This research is just getting started, so we do not yet know what the samples might reveal. That uncertainty is precisely why the work matters. We may detect antimicrobial resistance mechanisms that are already familiar to us, or resistances that we have not detected in the UK. We may find that risks vary according to the type or origin of a product. We may also learn important lessons about the practicality of border sampling and metagenomic surveillance. Whatever the findings, the project has the potential to give us a clearer view of a currently underexplored route into the UK.

This is what One Health action looks like in practice: scientists, policymakers, border professionals and industry working together across organisational boundaries. By combining new technology with existing expertise, we can improve our ability to spot potential threats early and make decisions based on evidence.
AMR is a shared challenge. Understanding how it moves is one of the first steps towards stopping it.

title: Commercial arrangements for digital proof of age for alcohol

content.content: The Licensing Act 2003 (Mandatory Licensing Conditions) (Amendment) Order 2026 is now in force. It enables licensed premises and club premises with a certificate in England and Wales to accept digital proof of age when selling or supplying alcohol, provided they comply with the legal requirements and any local licensing conditions.

One of the requirements under the legislation is that the “responsible person” for the licensed premises or premises holding a club premises certificate must be covered by an agreement with a registered digital verification service provider (“DVSP”) for the provision of digital verification services. The legislation calls this provider the “relevant DVSP”.

Our previous posts have explored how digital proof of age can work for alcohol sales from a number of different angles. In this blog post, we look at another area that providers and businesses interested in digital proof of age for alcohol sales have asked us about: how the requirement for an agreement might apply to different technical and commercial models, including where more than one DVSP is involved.
The responsible person must be covered by an agreement with a registered DVSP

When a customer chooses to use a digital proof of age, the responsible person may accept it only where they are covered by an agreement with a registered DVSP for the provision of digital verification services.
Under the legislation, that agreement must include a requirement that the DVSP will deliver digital proof of age to the responsible person which:
In simple terms, a “level of confidence” indicates how sure the DVSP is that the customer is who they say they are. You can read more about the "medium" level of confidence in our previous blog.
You do not need separate agreements with customers’ DVSPs

Where more than one DVSP is involved in producing or checking a digital proof of age, the responsible person does not need to be covered by separate agreements with each DVSP. Instead, they must be covered by an agreement with the DVSP for delivery of digital proof of age.

The legislation recognises that the required level of confidence may have been verified either by the DVSP delivering the digital proof of age to the responsible person, or by another registered DVSP.
Different technical and commercial models may involve multiple DVSPs. The legislation does not prescribe a particular model, provided the statutory requirements are met.

Where the verification of a digital form of identification involves one or more intermediary DVS, the statutory guidance recommends that the agreement between the licence or certificate holder and the delivering DVS makes it clear that any intermediary DVS must be a certified and registered DVS. This will help to provide reassurance that any digital form of identification meets the necessary requirements.
The legislation does not prescribe a particular form of contract
Neither the legislation nor the DVS trust framework specifies that the agreement must take the form of a freestanding, separately signed contract.
The requirement is that the responsible person is covered by an agreement with the relevant registered DVSP containing the necessary provisions.
Depending on the commercial model, those provisions may, for example, be incorporated into standard terms and conditions.
What matters is not the title or format of the document, but that the requirements in the legislation are met.
The legislation remains technology-neutral

The legislation sets out the conditions which must be met in order to accept digital proof of age in this context, but does not prescribe a specific technical approach for how licence and certificate holders implement these requirements in practice.

It also does not prescribe how contractual arrangements should be structured, as the appropriateness of particular contractual terms will depend on the specific circumstances and commercial arrangements of the parties involved. Organisations should consider their own circumstances and seek independent legal advice where appropriate.
This flexibility allows different technical and commercial models to develop while ensuring that the statutory safeguards continue to apply.

title: Healthcare innovation: making it work in the real world

content.content: Why do some innovations fail? Even the best inventions can be hindered when it comes to adoption, integration and delivery. This can happen when risk has not been assessed and addressed before an innovation is rolled out in the real world.There is no shortage of good ideas in healthcare. The difficult bit is turning them into something that genuinely works for patients, staff and the wider system.In his latest article, ACE Healthcare Customer Engagement Lead Waleed Backler explores what de-risking innovation means for the healthcare sector and why identifying risks, testing assumptions and learning early really matters.Read Waleed’s original article on LinkedIn – Post | LinkedInTrying something genuinely different will always bring some uncertainty.At ACE, we test how healthcare innovation can support earlier diagnosis, timely intervention and more personalised care across the UK. We work in areas where we don’t always have all the answers, so identifying risks, testing assumptions and learning early really matters.Innovation is not always invention.Too often innovation is confused with invention.Something can be new, exciting and technically impressive without necessarily solving the problem it was designed to address. Equally, innovation doesn’t always have to involve inventing something completely new.It can mean applying existing technology differently, bridging a gap, improving a pathway or simply finding a better way of tackling an age-old problem.So, we need to start with the challenge and who it affects, not the technology.Why does the problem exist? What are we trying to change? And what would better actually look like?Genuine innovation happens when those questions can be answered and the solution leads to something that can make a meaningful difference in the real world. But identifying the right problem and developing a promising solution is only part of the challenge. Getting it adopted, integrated and scaled across healthcare is another.Testing in the real worldA solution must work for the people using it and should function within existing pathways, infrastructure and current ways of working. Something that works well in one setting may not necessarily work in another, and understanding those differences is an important part of the innovation process.This is why testing matters, so we can focus on solving real-life operational challenges and challenges faced by clinicians and patients, rather than simply demonstrating that the technology works.Moving quickly shouldn’t mean deploying faster. It should mean testing assumptions, learning what works and adapting while there is still time to do so.We need to move from “this looks promising” to “we understand where and how this can work and how it will make a difference.”Understanding risk earlyUnderstanding the risks involved is an important part of that process, particularly for AI-enabled technologies.Risk doesn’t suddenly appear at the point of deployment, and our understanding of it shouldn’t start or stop there either.Crucially, this isn’t about creating another barrier to innovation. It’s about understanding the risks early enough to adjust and make better decisions. Sometimes discovering quickly that an approach isn’t going to work is a valuable outcome in itself.That means starting with the problem, involving the right expertise early, testing assumptions in real-world settings and building evidence and learning into the process.Because if we only assess risk when a solution is ready to deploy, we may already have left it too late.

title: Our Chief Executive’s speech to the Institute of Grocery Distribution (12 November 2026)

content.content: FSA Chief Executive Katie Pettifer addressed the Institute of Grocery Distribution’s Food Safety and Resilience Conference on Thursday 12 November.

Katie argued that as food safety risks become more complex, interconnected and unpredictable, the UK food system must shift from reacting to incidents to preventing them through better intelligence, risk-based regulation, and close collaboration between industry, government and regulators.
Speech as follows:
‘Building a More Resilient Food System: Collaboration, Prevention and Preparedness in Times of Volatility’
Good morning, everyone. It's a pleasure to be here with many familiar faces, and hopefully a chance to meet many more of you today.
The people in this room keep the food system running, day in, day out. So, first of all, thank you for the great work you do, and for the chance to spend some time with you this morning.

I’m not going to say anything today that you don’t already know.  The collective knowledge of the food system in this room is vast.  But I will try to set out how we’re looking at food system resilience at the FSA, and how we can work together with others in government, with local authorities and with you to achieve it.

Because resilience in the food system is a topic which informs so much of what we do: from future food regulation to approving innovative new food products for the market. For us, resilience and food safety go hand in hand - and I think that’s a good place to start.
Why resilience matters more than ever

Ten or fifteen years ago the operating environment for the food system felt a bit more predictable. Incidents, costs, and competition have, of course, always been part of the landscape, but pressures perhaps felt steadier and more predictable. But that's not the world we're in anymore.

Global shocks to the system have become the new normal. What used to feel exceptional is becoming routine. Whether it’s geopolitical instability disrupting trade and supply; economic pressure on businesses and households, or climate-related impacts on agricultural production. Food safety risks are emerging, and evolving, ever more rapidly.
I know that none of this is news to you, but let me put some numbers around it, because I think they're striking.

Last year, the FSA dealt with more than 1,800 food and feed safety incidents, while monitoring more than 12,500 intelligence signals across the food system. While that overall volume has stayed broadly stable, compared to previous years, the complexity and scale of incidents is rising year on year.  We classify the incidents we deal with as low, medium or high priority.  A few years ago, I’d have been telling you that the low-priority incidents were the largest group.  Last year around 90% were medium or high.

It’s not only incidents that are becoming more complex. Recent trends in foodborne disease point to growing underlying pressures in the system. The FSA's latest analysis confirmed that two of the four key pathogens we monitor, Campylobacter and Salmonella, exceeded our established thresholds for action, which has led to further investigation into the causes of those increases.
Together, these pathogens are responsible for more than 330,000 foodborne illnesses each year in the UK, with significant impacts on public health and the economy.

This picture is reinforced by recent incidents. This year, for example, we’ve taken action in response to an outbreak of Salmonella Enteritidis linked to imported eggs from a supplier in Ukraine, which triggered product withdrawals and recalls across the supply chain.
Our engagement through the international food safety network, INFOSAN, is also up too, from 987 notifications to 1,147.

Today's incidents increasingly cross organisational, geographic, and national boundaries. They pull in microbiologists, toxicologists, risk assessors, local authorities, international regulators and industry partners, often all at once, rather than sitting neatly within one business or one location.
A few examples from the last couple of years bring this to life better than any statistic.

The first is the E. coli outbreak linked to salad leaves which happened in 2024. The FSA and UKHSA investigated an outbreak of STEC O145 that was ultimately traced to lettuce used in ready-to-eat products. This was the largest ever STEC outbreak on record in the UK.

Two hundred and seventy-five cases were reported across the UK. Forty-nine per cent of those people were hospitalised. Seven people developed haemolytic uraemic syndrome and sadly two people died. These aren’t just statistics, they’re real lives.

A single ingredient, appearing in sandwiches, wraps and salads supplied through numerous retailers and manufacturers, meant that growers, processors, manufacturers, retailers, local authorities, UKHSA and the FSA all had to work together, at pace. Multiple product withdrawals and recalls followed across the country.

The outbreak also highlighted areas where we needed to improve, and since then the FSA and industry have worked closely together to apply the lessons learned, strengthen prevention measures and enhance our ability to detect and respond to emerging risks. I'm confident that those improvements are making a difference.

The second example is the peanut contamination of mustard ingredients which we were dealing with last year. This incident, for me, is a clear illustration of just how interconnected this system has become.
Mustard ingredients supplied by one relatively small-scale company turned out to be potentially contaminated with peanut. A clear risk, obviously, to those with an allergy.

Those ingredients were already in spice blends, seasonings, ready meals, sauces, snacks, foodservice products and retail own-brand lines. An issue with one ingredient, cascading through multiple tiers of the supply chain, triggered an exceptionally large recall programme across many brands and retailers. This incident alone contributed to a 55% increase in FSA allergy alerts for that year.

This was not just a contamination incident. It exposed a vulnerability in the system itself: we could not reliably trace the affected batches through the supply chain, and certainly not quickly enough, forcing us to advise people with a peanut allergy to avoid all products containing mustard.

And once again, this year, we were reminded how wide-reaching a failure early in the supply chain can be, when contamination was identified in arachidonic acid oil supplied from China, an ingredient used in the manufacture of infant formula. Its effects were felt across the global market because multiple manufacturers relied on the same supplier for this ingredient.

It showed us that modern food systems are not only complex and globally interconnected but can also be dependent on a limited number of suppliers. When those single points of failure emerge, the consequences can quickly spread across supply chains, reducing resilience and affecting supply.

These incidents highlight an emerging reality for food regulation: resilience is no longer just about managing individual risks but understanding how risks interact across complex systems. Common dependencies can create hidden vulnerabilities, meaning that a failure in one supplier, ingredient or process can have system-wide consequences.

Building resilience therefore requires us to look beyond individual businesses and products to better understand the interconnected nature of modern supply chains, identify critical points of dependence and work collectively to manage the risks they create.

This isn’t just a passing phase. If we look ahead at potential future pressures, particularly the impact of extreme weather on agricultural production and supply availability it's clear that resilience will be vital to meet new challenges head-on.
What do we mean by food system resilience?
Before I go further, it's worth pausing on what we actually mean by resilience, because all of us in this room may be looking at it through a slightly different lens.

If you run a food business, resilience probably means commercial and financial resilience: can you keep operating, keep supplying, keep trading through disruption. If you're a technical leader, it probably means supply chain integrity and operational continuity: can you trust what's coming into your business and keep it moving safely.
At the FSA, our lens is food safety, authenticity and consumer protection: can people trust that the food on the shelves is safe, is what it says it is, and is accessible.
These are different lenses, looking at the same system. At the FSA we find it useful to think about this in three layers:
There's global resilience: the wider environment of climate, politics, energy markets, transport and infrastructure, much of which sits outside any single organisation's control.
There's food system resilience: the ability of the system as a whole to anticipate, absorb and adapt to disruption.
And there's food safety resilience, which is the FSA’s particular focus within that: safe, authentic food, and reliable consumer protection.

In terms of resilience, the question we all need to address is not whether future shocks will occur. We know they will. The question is whether we build a system capable of withstanding them and recovering quickly when they do.
Five building blocks of a resilient food system
So let me set out how I think we do that. I want to talk about five building blocks. None of these will be new to you, but I think the combination is important.
First: better intelligence and horizon scanning
In a food system that’s becoming more complex, interconnected and exposed to global shocks, we need a stronger understanding of the risks that may emerge in the months and years ahead.

That means investing in data, scientific evidence, international networks and analytical capability to identify changing patterns, detect early warning signs and understand what is coming down the track.

Whether the challenge comes from foodborne disease, climate change, geopolitical disruption, technological innovation or changing consumer behaviours, our ability to anticipate risk will increasingly determine our ability to respond effectively.

Building resilience starts with seeing risks sooner and understanding their potential impact.  It’s one of the areas where new technology has huge potential to help us – we've got tools available now that can help us analyse data and make connections at a far greater scale than we could ever do before.
But horizon scanning isn’t something we can do in isolation, because these risks don’t fall into neat boxes.  The drivers of risk, and the consequences, cut across organisational boundaries.

For example, the risks to food safety are often indivisible from risks to food supply.  So, the FSA and Defra need to work as one on this within Government, and with our colleagues in Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
Second: Regulation that uses intelligence effectively

Gathering information is only valuable if it informs action. The goal is not simply to identify risks, but to use data and insight to prevent harm, target interventions where they are needed most, and take action before issues escalate into incidents.
This means applying intelligence-led and risk-based regulation, focusing resources on the areas of greatest concern while reducing unnecessary burdens elsewhere.

The development of the FSA's new food standards delivery model reflects this approach, using better data and intelligence to support more targeted, proportionate and effective regulatory interventions. By acting earlier and more precisely, we can strengthen consumer protection while making the regulatory system more resilient and responsive to change.​​​​
Third: stronger preparedness

How well you've prepared determines how well you respond to a risk in the system. We're reviewing and strengthening our own resilience planning, building readiness for increasingly complex incidents, and developing stronger cross-government and cross-sector coordination.

But I want to flag a new ambition here specifically: we want to exercise with industry, not just within government. Testing our assumptions together, before a crisis, rather than discovering the gaps in the middle of one.

That takes your participation in joint exercises and a willingness to share learning openly, including the challenging lessons. Preparedness can’t be built during an emergency. It has to be built beforehand and built together.
Fourth: effective incident management and response

Even the most resilient system will experience unexpected events, the examples I opened with prove that. We're continually improving our response capability, learning systematically from incidents, and improving coordination and decision-making. We've built on some genuinely successful collaborative work with industry and with IGD already.

Incident management is wider than just the immediate action taken in incidents. The most critical part, if we’re to strengthen resilience, is to take the learnings from each incident and use them to embed prevention throughout the food and animal feed chain.
Fifth: partnership, trust and shared responsibility
All of the previous four building blocks depends on this one.

We need to understand different perspectives. As we’ve been discussing, we each view resilience through a different lens, and understanding each other's view makes our collaboration stronger, not weaker.
Building trusted information sharing is vital. I know there are real commercial sensitivities we need to be conscious of, and I don't underestimate the significance of this.

But we need to keep developing trusted ways of sharing information that will strengthen the resilience of the whole system, not just one part of it. Recognising that actions in one part of the system have consequences elsewhere, often far from where they originated. No single organisation sees the whole picture alone.

On our side, that means continuing to build stronger partnerships, creating forums for collaboration like this one, and working with you to address shared risks directly. What we need from you is early engagement, openness, trust, and a willingness to solve problems jointly rather than at arm's length.
From response to prevention
Assembling those five building blocks together, I want to put them in a strategic context.

Resilience conversations have historically focused heavily on response: how do we react well when something goes wrong. That remains important, and I'm not suggesting we stop investing in it. But increasingly, our collective effort has to be directed towards prevention, early warning, and early intervention.
A resilient food system isn't one that simply responds well to crises. It's one that prevents more of those crises from happening in the first place.
That shift to prevention is something we want to support in the FSA, and we want to do that in partnership with Defra, with colleagues across the UK and with everyone in this room.
What we're asking of you
So let me turn that into something more concrete. I have three practical asks.
First, help us build stronger intelligence. Continue sharing your insights, your evidence, and your early sight of emerging risks. You often see things before we do.
Second, help us strengthen preparedness. Over the coming months and years, work with us, and others in government, to test and exercise our plans together, before we need them for real.

Third, help us deepen trust and find better ways to share information. We need to build a shared understanding of risk across the system, even where that information feels commercially sensitive. That trust has to be built in advance. It's tested in the moment, but it's built long before the incident occurs.
Conclusion
The pressures on this system are not going away. Volatility is becoming the new normal, not a temporary disruption to business as usual.
No regulator can solve that alone. No business or trade body can either. But together, we can build a system that's more resilient, better prepared, better informed and better connected.

The future resilience of our food system won't be determined by how any of us act alone. It will be determined by how effectively we work together to anticipate risk, prevent harm, and protect consumers.
Thank you.

title: Safeguarding Should Help Us Live the Lives We Want

content.content: Safeguarding should help us live the lives we want - blog by Dr Clenton Farquharson CBE
I am someone who draws on care and support and a former carer for my late mum. I employ personal assistants who help me live my life on my own terms.

Feeling safe, for me, means being able to speak honestly without fear, ask for help without judgement, and have control over my everyday life. Safeguarding decisions affect our homes, relationships and freedom. A safeguarding plan should help me feel safe while protecting my relationships, choices and freedom.
On the theme of co-production and shared decision-making, my starting point is simple: people must have real influence over decisions about their own lives.
Start with the person and their life
“How do we keep this person safe?” is an understandable question. But it can lead to decisions being made before we have understood the person and what they stand to lose.
I want us to ask together: “What matters to you? What helps you feel safe? What are you worried about? How can we support you to live the life you want?”

For me, that includes being in my own home, spending time with family, contributing through work and making everyday choices. If a proposed plan made it harder to see my family or leave home, I would want people to understand what I would lose and explore alternatives with me.
Being heard must lead to influence

Co-production means sharing power over how concerns are understood, what options are considered and what happens next. Inviting me to a meeting is a beginning. Can my contribution change the decision?

I need information in a format that works for me, time to understand the options, and communication support where needed. I may want someone I trust alongside me. These arrangements should help me express my own wishes.
I want to know how my views shaped the plan. If something I ask for cannot happen, explain why and explore alternatives with me.

It can be difficult to challenge someone whose help you depend on every day. I need confidence that raising concerns will be taken seriously and will not lead to threats about losing support. Disagreeing with a plan should prompt a conversation about my reasons, rather than an assumption that I am being difficult.
Stay alongside us when decisions are difficult

There will be difficult situations involving coercion or serious harm. Practitioners carry real responsibilities, and I recognise the judgement their work requires. Sharing decisions does not mean we will always agree.

If you believe action is necessary, explain your concerns, what alternatives have been considered, what choices remain and how I can challenge the decision. Keep listening to what matters to me throughout.
My life, relationships and support needs can change. I want to know who will stay in touch, when we will review the plan, and what will happen if it makes my life harder.
Judge success by what changes in our lives

A safeguarding process can end while someone still feels frightened, isolated or unheard. Ask me whether I feel safer, whether I have kept the relationships that matter, and whether I have more control over my life. Ask whether anything done in the name of safety has made life harder.

Our influence should also extend to designing safeguarding services and deciding how success is judged. When I share my experience to help improve services, I want support to do so and honest feedback about what changed.
Making Safeguarding Personal

This is what Making Safeguarding Personal means to me: protecting people from harm while making sure they have a real say in what happens next. A simple place to start is to ask,“what would feeling safer look like for you?”. We should then come back to that question, not just at the end of a safeguarding process, but throughout, to understand what has changed and whether the person feels safer, more in control and heard.
For anyone wanting to keep this approach at the heart of their practice, these resources may be helpful:

For me, person-shaped safeguarding starts with my life, relationships and communication needs, and shapes support around them. Its success should be felt in everyday life: greater safety, dignity, connection and the freedom to live a gloriously ordinary life.

title: Understanding Annex 1: A Harmonised Approach to Interpretation

content.content: The harmonised PIC/S-EMA-WHO interpretation of the most important changes in Annex 1 on the manufacture of sterile products (2022) has now been published. In this blog post, Graham Carroll (Lead Senior GMDP Inspector and PIC/S Annex 1 Implementation Working Group member) highlights what this means for pharmaceutical manufacturers.

The 2022 revision of Annex 1 represented a significant development in GMP expectations for the manufacture of sterile medicinal products. Since its publication, industry and regulators have been applying those requirements across a wide range of facilities, technologies, and manufacturing processes.

Following the introduction of the Annex 1 revision, a Joint Implementation Working Group was established, bringing together members from the Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme (PIC/S), European Medicines Agency (EMA) and World Health Organization (WHO). One of its objectives was to support a harmonised interpretation of the revised Annex 1. PIC/S has now published PI 058-1: Interpretation of the most important changes in the Annex 1 on the manufacture of sterile products (2022). The document entered into force on 28 October 2026 and brings together answers to important questions arising from the revision and implementation of Annex 1.

As a member of the working group, I am proud to have contributed to its development and to see the results of that considerable collective effort now published. This is a clear example of how the MHRA collaborates with trusted partners to actively shape global regulatory practice.
Why is the document important for pharmaceutical manufacturers?

Although the document has been developed to support a harmonised inspection approach, the working group was also keen that the interpretations should be accessible to industry. Inspections are an important part of protecting patient safety, but manufacturers should not have to wait until their next inspection to understand how aspects of Annex 1 are being interpreted. By publishing the document, manufacturers can consider those interpretations proactively and review their approach where appropriate, rather than first encountering an issue during an inspection.

PIC/S is clear that the purpose of PI 058-1 is not to introduce any new GMP requirements, nor does the document override the requirements of Annex 1, which remains the underlying requirement. The Q&A supports a harmonised approach to inspection by providing interpretations of some of the most important changes introduced in the 2022 revision. The document does not attempt to address every change made to Annex 1, but focuses on key questions arising during the revision process and following implementation.

The value of the Q&A is not as another checklist to place alongside Annex 1. Instead, it provides an opportunity for manufacturers to consider how they have interpreted and implemented Annex 1 and to compare their reasoning with the interpretations developed through the joint international working group.
Look beyond the individual answers
I am deliberately not going to summarise each of the questions and answers here. I would strongly encourage manufacturers to read the PIC/S publication itself.

The questions cover a broad range of practical issues across sterile manufacture, including the Contamination Control Strategy (CCS), facilities and cleanrooms, barrier technologies, personnel qualification, sterilisation, aseptic processing and interventions, sterilising filtration, single-use systems, environmental monitoring, and microbiological control.

There is considerable technical detail behind some of the answers, and reading them alongside the corresponding paragraphs of Annex 1 is more useful than looking at individual statements in isolation.

One theme that comes through strongly is the relationship between Quality Risk Management (QRM), scientific knowledge, and the CCS. Annex 1 provides scope for risk-based approaches in several areas, but the answers repeatedly illustrate the importance of understanding the underlying risk and having appropriate scientific or technical justification. The detail and use of the CCS similarly runs through many of the answers rather than appearing as a standalone exercise.
Using the Q&A in practice

For manufacturers, I would suggest reading PI 058-1 with your own operation in mind rather than simply reviewing it as a regulatory update. Where a question is relevant to your processes, consider the corresponding Annex 1 requirement and whether the interpretation should prompt you to revisit your current approach, its rationale or the evidence supporting it.

That does not mean that every example in the Q&A becomes an additional GMP requirement, nor that doing something differently automatically represents a deficiency. It does, however, provide a useful opportunity to challenge established assumptions within your organisation.

That could include looking again at how QRM has been applied, whether the CCS reflects current process knowledge and monitoring data, whether qualification and validation evidence supports the controls being relied upon, and whether the rationale behind important contamination-control decisions can be clearly explained.
Those are useful questions for any manufacturer to ask itself, independently of an inspection.
Not the end of the story

Despite the considerable work that has gone into this document, there will inevitably be areas that prompt further questions or where future interpretation may be helpful. This is version 1 of the document, and feedback from inspectors and industry will provide valuable input when future revisions are considered.

Inspections are not intended to be the forum for detailed feedback on the document itself. Industry feedback should instead be provided through the appropriate regulatory channels. For UK stakeholders, feedback can be submitted to the PIC/S Secretariat at info@picscheme.org, with the subject “Annex 1 Interpretation document”. It is particularly helpful if feedback identifies the relevant paragraph or question, clearly describes the issue, and provides a technically supported proposal or rationale.
A considerable collective effort

The relatively short final document inevitably hides the scale of the work behind it. It is no exaggeration to say that thousands of hours of discussion, drafting, review and technical consideration went into reaching the final document. That considerable collective effort reflected a shared objective; to provide useful interpretations that support greater consistency in how the revised Annex 1 is understood and applied.

I hope manufacturers will also benefit from the extensive work that went into this document. It is a relatively concise read, but one that should prompt some worthwhile conversations about how Annex 1 has been implemented in practice. I would encourage manufacturers to read the Q&A in full, consider the questions relevant to their operations and use them as an opportunity to reflect on their own implementation of Annex 1.

title: Listening & Person-Centred Conversations (starting with listening)

content.content: Introduction from Sarah McClinton

I’m very pleased to start Safeguarding Adults Week by introducing our first of a series of blogs from members of the National Adult Safeguarding Board. Thank you to Lucy Rush, Principal Social Worker (PSW) at Hertfordshire County Council and co-chair of the Adult PSW network for sharing this moving and very personal reflection. Through the experience of her uncle Pete, Lucy reminds us that losing the ability to speak should not mean losing your voice, your identity or your right to be heard. Her story is a powerful reminder of why we must look beyond spoken words, listen in all the ways people communicate and make sure the person remains at the heart of safeguarding.
What does it mean to truly listen? Blog by Lucy Rush

In safeguarding, we talk about giving people a voice and Making Safeguarding Personal, yet for many people, expressing those wishes, concerns and experiences is not straightforward. Communication is more than spoken words; it is how we make sense of the world, build relationships, express choices and seek help when we need it.
Effective safeguarding practice starts with genuine curiosity, active listening and a commitment to hearing the person irrespective of their circumstances.

During Safeguarding Adults Week, it feels particularly important to recognise that we still have a long way to go. Learning from Safeguarding Adult Reviews, Ombudsman investigations, legal cases and challenge raised by national organisations consistently shows that people are placed at greater risk of abuse, neglect, self-neglect and poor outcomes when their communication needs are not recognised or adapted for.

Opportunities to prevent or reduce harm can be missed when professionals have relied on others to speak on a person's behalf, failed to adapt practice to individuals’ communication, or overlooked non-verbal expressions of distress and fear.
Communication is not simply a professional skill; it is a safeguarding intervention

Why have I chosen to talk about this today? After 28 years working in social care, there hasn’t been a single day where communicating and listening to people hasn’t been the single most important and enjoyable part of my job. Communication is fundamental to how I navigate the world and how I make my voice heard. People (sometimes!) listen to me…they hear what I have to say, they respond to me and there is a sense of equity in the conversation. But what happens if you lose this skill?  Does it fundamentally change you as a person or does it just change the perception of those around you.

For me, a personal experience makes me want to challenge and champion listening and communicating. In 2023 my Uncle Pete experienced a brain aneurism. Following an emergency operation from which he initially recovered, he was medically cleared and was ready to be discharged home with a few lifestyle changes. He was visited by his daughter in hospital, and they spoke about him looking forward to getting home. He told her he loved her, and these were the last words he was ever able to say out loud.

His condition rapidly deteriorated and he was left paralysed and non-verbal. He couldn’t talk, he couldn’t move, but he could very clearly think for himself, make decisions about his life and he could communicate. One of the most difficult experiences for him was navigating the world when people assume because he couldn't speak, he didn’t have a voice. Uncle Pete had a voice; it just didn't come out of his mouth.

After everything that had been physically taken away from him, it was imperative that he maintained agency over his own words, his own feelings and that people listen. At its worst, he was asked to “blink” at a housing officer to end his tenancy, not: contact his established communication support. Not: use the augmentative and alternative communication system he has in place. Not: ask the people who know how he communicates to support with facilitating a conversation. Just... blink, if you agree.

And then there have been the safeguarding concerns; from being left alone in a room on a ward for hours and hours in pain, struggling for oxygen, freezing cold… from no one thinking to ask him what he needed because he couldn’t speak… to no one considering why he didn’t press the alarm for help because he couldn’t move. Words cannot express how demoralising this is for a man with full capacity and who is the same person he has always been. Strong, northern, stubborn, loving, funny…exactly the same, just told his stories in a different way.

To truly listen, to hear a person’s voice and to make it central to making safeguarding personal please challenge yourselves every day to make sure you are doing everything you should and can to make sure that person is heard. Build on your awareness of augmentative and alternative communication and always ask what someone's communication method is so that you can listen to them and make listening and communication an intervention in its own right.
In loving memory of our wonderful Uncle Pete.

title: A simple update that can help protect your property from fraud
authors: Lynne Feddon, Head of Counter Fraud

content.content: When you move home or change your contact details, updating the details held on your property’s title register may not be at the top of your list. But this simple step can make a real difference if someone tries to make an application involving your property.

HM Land Registry uses your contact details – known as your ‘address for service’ – when we need to write to you about your property. If they are out of date, an important notice may not reach you when it matters.
This is one of the actions we are highlighting during International Fraud Awareness Week, when organisations around the world share practical ways to guard against fraud.

Property fraud remains relatively rare, but the impact can be serious. A fraudster may steal a property owner’s identity and use forged documents to try to sell or mortgage a property without the rightful owner knowing. This is known as registered title fraud.

HM Land Registry prevented 63 fraudulent applications in 2025/26, protecting property worth more than £63 million. These cases represented a very small proportion of the millions of applications we received, but behind every attempted fraud is a person or business facing potential financial loss, disruption and distress.
Why contact details matter

That's why being a registered proprietor really helps, providing us with at least one address and adding up to three contact details for the register, including another postal address or an email address.

Having more than one reliable contact route is particularly useful if you rent out a property, own a commercial property, live overseas, spend long periods away or manage property on behalf of a company. It is also worth checking each property you own, rather than assuming the contact details held by us are all the same.
A notice that stopped a fraudulent application

In one significant recent case, HM Land Registry received an application to register a commercial charge, or mortgage, worth more than £467,000 against a property in London. We were able to reach the proprietor at another address we had listed. They confirmed they had been the victim of identity fraud, so the application was cancelled.
Checking the title register among simple steps to help protect your property

To help protect your property, check and update the contact details shown on the title register for each address, including when you move or change email address; consider adding more than one way for us to reach you; make sure any email address you provide is monitored, including junk or spam folders; and act promptly if we contact you about an application you don’t recognise.
You can update a registered owner’s contact address using form COG1 and there is no fee for this service. Our YouTube video: How to update your contact address can help guide you through the process.
Sign up to Property Alert and ‘restriction on title’ for peace of mind

You can also sign up for HM Land Registry’s free Property Alert service. This service will email you about certain activity on a property you are monitoring, including applications to change the register. You can monitor up to 10 registered properties in England and Wales.

A ‘restriction on title’, or Form LL restriction, can also be an option if needed. This can require a conveyancer to certify that the person selling or mortgaging the property is the registered owner before the transaction can be registered. For more information on the pros and cons of Form LL restrictions, see our blog: Protecting your property from fraud: Form LL – the ‘counter-fraud’ restriction, or our YouTube video.
Other ways HM Land Registry helps prevent fraud, working across Government

HM Land Registry works throughout the year to protect the integrity of the register. Caseworkers check that the necessary documents are present and in order, and refer applications that do not look right to specialist colleagues. Our Counter Fraud Group reviews suspicious activity, supports caseworkers and works with partners across government and the property sector to understand emerging threats.

No single check can remove every risk. Information from owners can be crucial, and a quick response to a notice or Property Alert may help us identify an application that needs closer attention before a change is made to the register.
Don’t forget, if something does not look right, it may not be right
Not every letter or alert will mean fraud and there may be a legitimate application in progress, for example after a sale, remortgage or change of name.

However, if you are signed up to Property Alert and receive a notice or alert about activity you do not recognise, please don’t ignore it. Follow the contact details provided and get in touch with HM Land Registry as soon as possible.
You can also contact us if you think you’re the victim of property fraud, email reportafraud@landregistry.gov.uk or telephone: 0300 006 7030 Monday to Friday (excluding Bank Holidays), 8am to 4.30pm.
You should also consider getting independent legal advice and reporting the matter to the police’s national fraud reporting service, Report Fraud, on 0300 123 2040.
Avoid being the victim of property fraud during IFAW 26 and at all times.
One small task, an important safeguard

Fraudsters can use stolen identities and forged documents to target property. HM Land Registry has safeguards in place, but property owners have an important part to play too. Take a few minutes to check the contact details held for your property. Keeping them up to date could help us reach you when it matters most.

title: Learning the ancient art of coppicing

content.content: The Bill Hogarth Memorial Apprenticeship Trust was established in 2001. It honours the legacy of Bill Hogarth, a coppice merchant who worked the woods of Cumbria for 56 years. Bill was known for his generosity as a teacher and in 1995 received an MBE for his contributions to the coppice industry. Following his death in 1999, friends and colleagues set up a charity to further his work, and to train the future generation of coppice workers.
The Bill Hogarth Memorial Apprenticeship scheme

As a former apprentice graduate and now sponsor, mentor, coppicer and Chair at the Trust, I have the pleasure to witness how each new cohort of apprentices develop the necessary skills and knowledge needed to continue Bill Hogarth’s legacy.

In this 3-year apprenticeship scheme, our apprentices learn about coppicing alongside a sponsor in their coppice business. They receive a bursary and budgets to complete the course and learn how to set up their own coppice business. Upon completion, our successful apprentices are awarded ‘The Bill Hogarth Coppice Diploma’.

As the Apprentice Co-ordinator, I am at present supporting the Trust’s 6 coppicing apprentices. In this blog you will hear more about what they have learnt and their experiences throughout their time on the apprenticeship scheme.
The ancient art of coppicing
Coppicing is an ancient and sustainable woodland management technique for broadleaf trees or shrubs, dating back to the 13th century.

Hardwood trees are cut to ground level during the winter. As their root network remains intact, they’ll send up multiple shoots from the cut stump (the 'stool') and regrow the following spring. These are usually left for a few years (depending on the species), and then the process repeats as a way of sustainably harvesting the wood for many different products. These products are traditionally used for various woodcrafts. It’s believed woods have been coppiced since the Neolithic period, which has allowed habitat to develop alongside woodland work.
Tree protection

While regrowth is fresh it’s easily damaged which can lead to poor quality products. Damaged shoots grow back branching and bent, whereas straight stems are ideal for most coppice products. Severe damage can lead to the death of the root system or the whole tree. To prevent this, it’s common to put deer fencing around newly cut areas of coppice until the growth is too high for deer to reach. Another strategy is to control the deer population in the area.
Geographical differences

There are really interesting differences in coppicing across the country. For example, on a limestone pavement in Silverdale (north-west Lancashire), there aren’t many nutrients, so you can cut there on a 10-year rotation. Whereas, in Greater Manchester, you can cut hazel on a 7-year rotation.

There’s also quite a difference between the standards of species. Down south, for example, there’s lots of cherry and sweet chestnut which you don’t see as much of up north. And on limestone pavement there’s a lot more yew and blackthorn, which shows the diversity of what a coppice coup can look like.
The benefits of coppicing
Boosting biodiversity

Coppicing boosts biodiversity in a variety of ways and supports woodland flora and fauna. Cutting coppice creates cycles of light and shade on the woodland floor, which can be really beneficial for a variety of plants and animals. A greater amount of light getting to the woodland floor allows ground flora species (for example primrose, the food for rare fritillary butterflies) to thrive, and vines such as honeysuckle, are essential for dormice.

Coppicing helps to create mosaic woodland as they typically combine open scrub and grasslands to create vital edge habitats. Freshly cut coppice can look a little scary since the stools are cut right to the ground, but the following years of growth create a beautiful mosaic woodland of different life stages of the hazel tree.
Supporting the local economy
Coppicing can provide many benefits to the local economy which in turn supports the forestry sector. Coppicing supports the local economy by:
Sustainability

Coppicing is sustainable because when you cut trees down to the ground it enables the remaining stump (stool) to rapidly grow multiple stems in a repeating cycle every 7 to 20 years (depending on the species). Coppicing produces renewable material on a short rotation with minimal impact on the environment.
Remarkable, coppiced wood products

We asked our apprentices what they have made from coppiced wood during their time on the apprenticeship scheme. Their responses highlight the sheer variety of products you can make from this ancient form of woodland management.

The next generation of coppicers

By continuing this ancient management technique and investing in the next generation of skilled workers, we can continue to support biodiversity, produce renewable materials, strengthen local economies and create resilient, thriving woodlands for the future.

As Chair, I am proud that our apprenticeship scheme is supporting the next generation of skilled coppice workers to ensure coppiced woodlands remain a valuable part of our landscape for years to come.
